News.title: F-16 crash - live: US fighter jet explodes in Michigan during training exercise
News.content:
The F-16 was carrying out a routine training mission when it crashed

An F-16 fighter jet has crashed in Grand Traverse County, Michigan, with images from the scene showing a massive fire engulfing debris in a field

An F-16 fighter jet has crashed in Grand Traverse County, Michigan - moments after its pilot ejected and parachuted to safety.

The crash happened at around 2pm EDT (7pm BST) near County Road 633, between Jeffrey Place and Blair Townhall Road, in Green Lake Township. Dramatic images from the scene show a large fire and thick smoke rising from the wreckage.

The aircraft belonged to the Texas Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Wing and was carrying out a routine training mission, the Texas Military Department said. Sgt Derek Gutierrez, of the 149th Fighter Wing, said the pilot is receiving medical treatment at a local hospital.

Traffic has been blocked and motorists have been urged to avoid the area. A shelter-in-place order has been issued for residents nearby.

News.title: BBC Question Time erupts into laughter as Danny Kruger defends £72 million Reform UK donations
News.content:
BBC Question Time erupts into laughter as Danny Kruger defends £72 million Reform UK donations

Question Time returns for a new series from Salisbury, with politicians, commentators and members of the public debating topics including the threat of artificial intelligence on mankind and the £72m donations received by Reform UK

View 4 Images Reform UK’s Danny Kruger could not keep a straight face when trying to defend the donations (Image: BBC Question Time)

Reform UK’s Danny Kruger was grilled over the party's £72 million donations on tonight's Question Time.

‌



Colossal donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, two cryptocurrency billionaires who until recently lived in Hong Kong and Thailand respectively caused quiet the debate on BBC Question Time tonight.

‌



Tonight's show, hosted in Sailsbury, featured the transport secretary Heidi Alexander; the shadow minister for women and equalities Joy Morrissey; Reform UK’s Danny Kruger and the former leader of the Green Party Caroline Lucas.

‌



View 4 Images (Image: BBC Question Time)

An audience member named Stella Smith asked "Is the £72million in donations received by Reform this week a threat to democracy?" To which Caroline Lucas responded: "Yes, it is a massive threat to democracy. It really does look as if it's the case that British democracy is up for sale to the highest bidder and that frankly is obscene and we should be sending a very clear message to say that British democracy is not for sale."

She added: "I don't think the British public are the fools that Reform seems to take them for so we really need to clean this up."

‌



Reform UK’s Danny Kruger attempted to defend the party's donations but while doing so the audience erupted into laughter. He began by saying: "I think that it's an admirable thing that these two men, that will get nothing for it, no peerage, no policy, they're not getting anything for it. There's absolutely nothing in it for them. They are British voters registered here, British citizens who have made their money, they've been passed by the electoral commission as permitted donors to political parties so I'm afraid it's absolutely great that they've done so because they've given Reform a chance to stand up against the established parties."

View 4 Images Stella Smith found the Reform MP's explanation hilarious (Image: BBC Question Time)

Danny was then questioned by Joy Morrissey about Nigel Farage's personal gift of £5million at which point the audience erupted into laughter once again.

‌



The Reform MP said: "So that was a personal gift given to him before he was a politician.and completely consistent with the rules." While in the background a panelist can be heard saying: "He can't even say it with a straight face."

Host Fiona has to interject saying: "Hang on, when you say it's consistent with the rules it is being assessed as to if it is consistent or not."

Transport secretary Heidi Alexander was then asked if her issue was the size of the donations or the face they made the donations at all. She said: "I believe that there should be a cap in place and that is the change we are making through the elections bill."

‌



After being questioned by Joy Morrissey about donations made by unions not being included in the donation cap Heidi said: "I think that trade unions play an important role in our society... I go back to the point I made previously, these are invidual donations that ordinary men and women decide to make through their trade union and I think that broadens the base of our democracy and I think that's a good thing for the country."

Ministers have already taken steps to introduce a £100,000 ceiling on the sum of money that can be donated to political parties by anyone living abroad, which would also be enforced for the first 12 months after British expats come back to the UK.

The changes would be backdated to March, prompting questions about whether Reform can retain the twin £36million contributions from Ben Delo, who was living in Hong Kong until recently, and Christopher Harborne, who was living in Thailand.

‌



View 4 Images Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has come under fire following the huge donations given to his political party (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Asked whether the donations would be affected by new rules on overseas donors, Mr Farage said: "Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever." Mr Farage then suggested they would no longer be permissible under changes proposed in the Representation of the People Bill, which has now entered committee stage.

When pressed on whether Mr Delo and Mr Harborne were UK residents as of March 25 — a detail that could have a direct bearing on the validity of their donations — he said: "I'm not going to go into their particular details.

Article continues below

"All I'm going to say is, with the law of the land as it stands, they are both compliant. Now, there is talk, and Angela Rayner was talking about this yesterday, there is talk of them retrospectively declaring donations illegally. Well, that simply cannot be."

BBC Question Time returns next week in Cambridge and again on Thursday, October 1 in North London.

News.title: Premier League star Leif Davis hailed for joining Noah Woods search and huge donation
News.content:
Premier League star Leif Davis hailed for joining Noah Woods search and huge donation

Leif Davis, who plays for Premier League club Ipswich, was among the 1,000-plus search party looking for three-year-old Noah Woods, whose body has now been found

View 3 Images Leif Davis has donated to the family of Noah Woods (Image: Richard Pelham/Getty Images)

Ipswich defender Leif Davis has been hailed for donating £2,000 to the family of Noah Woods. Davis, 26, is said to have been among the group of at least 1,300 volunteers who went looking for the three-year-old in the early hours of Wednesday morning.

‌



Noah went missing from a playground in Brantham, Suffolk, at around 3pm on Tuesday, having becoming separated from a relative. A body was discovered the following day in a lake known as Decoy Pond and police say that it had been formally identified.

‌



A Just Giving page has been set up by 'Good Dads Club' in support of the family, with more than £71,000 raised already. Davis kindly gave a £2,000 donation, receiving widespread praise on social media.

‌



"That's an amazing thing to do," one user posted on X. "A lovely bloke," another wrote.

‌



On the Just Giving page, an Ipswich fan said that Davis had joined the search shortly after Tuesday's clash with Arsenal in the Carabao Cup at Portman Road. "Leif came down to help with the search on Saturday (sic) straight after coming off the pitch," the supporter said. "Top class fella. Respect to Ipswich Town."

Ipswich paid tribute to Noah on Thursday. Club captain Dara O'Shea and goalkeeper Christian Walton also laid a wreath at the playground where he was last seen.

View 3 Images Police have identified Noah Woods' body (Image: Suffolk Police / SWNS)

‌



"The thoughts of everyone at Ipswich Town are with the family and friends of Noah Woods at this tragic time," the Premier League club said. "We will be wearing black armbands for this weekend's fixtures, in memory of Noah."

Ipswich's men's first-team will play away to Everton on Saturday. The Tractor Boys' next home game will be against Fulham on October 10 following the international break.

Noah's father, Rhys, said in a post on Facebook that his son 'will be loved forever' and nothing can describe the family's loss. Rhys said: "Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much.

‌



View 3 Images Leif Davis gave an incredible donation (Image: Just Giving)

"This was the most heartbreaking outcome for us, we were just hoping that he would be hiding somewhere obvious where someone could find him. That's what we kept telling ourselves the whole time."

He added: "It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation. You have all taken Noah into your own hearts, with all the overwhelming help, we were all just trying to bring him home to us safe and sound."

News.title: Greater Manchester school sends warning to parents as man seen recording pupil
News.content:
Greater Manchester school sends warning to parents as man seen recording pupil

A man described as 'bald and in his fifties or sixties' was reportedly spotted recording a pupil on Clover Road in Timperley, Greater Manchester, outside Wellington School

View Image The incident took place in the vicinity of Wellington School in Timperley (Image: Google Street View)

Parents of students at a school in Greater Manchester have been asked to be vigilant after a man was reportedly seen following and recording a pupil.

The incident allegedly took place outside Wellington School, a mixed secondary and sixth form in Timperley.

An email sent to parents described the man as "a bald male in his fifties or sixties".

The warning added that he appeared to be recording the student in question on his phone.

It read: "We want to make all parents and carers aware of a report that an adult male in the area was seen on Clover Road yesterday appearing to follow a student and record them with his phone.

Couple jailed over ‘depraved’ plans to sexually abuse young girl in Wales READ MORE :

Met Office names areas facing heavy rain on Friday with 19 counties at risk READ MORE :

"He has been described as a bald male in his fifties or sixties, wearing glasses and a dark tracksuit."

The school added that the incident has been reported to the police, Manchester Evening News reports.

The message continued: "Staff on the school gates have been alerted to this report so that they can remain vigilant as students are leaving site."

Parents have also been urged to contact the school should they have any further concerns and report any similar incidents to the police.

The concerning incident quickly attracted reaction from parents on social media, as the email was shared in an Altrincham Facebook group. The poster urged: "Please make your children aware."

One user replied: "These warnings feel far too frequent these days, so worrying."

Mirror Online has approached Greater Manchester Police for comment.

News.title: Families whose loved ones were 'groomed' into suicide demand Andy Burnham launch public inquiry
News.content:
Families whose loved ones were 'groomed' into suicide demand Andy Burnham launch public inquiry

Andy Burnham has been urged to launch a statutory public inquiry into the repeated failure to stop a suicide grooming forum linked to more than 130 deaths in the UK

View 2 Images Andy Burnham has been urged to launch a statutory public inquiry into 'repeated failures' to stop a suicide grooming forum (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Bereaved families and a survivor have called for a statutory public inquiry into repeated failures to stop a suicide grooming forum linked to more than 130 deaths in the UK.

‌



In a letter to Andy Burnham, the families of more than a dozen people - including children as young as 16 - who died between 2020 and 2025 have called for an inquiry to "expose the failures that cost their lives"

‌



The group, which also includes a survivor of the forum, said their loved ones were "drawn into a dark, nihilistic online world that continues to be easily accessible to this day".

‌



"They were groomed, exploited, instructed and actively encouraged to take their own lives," they said. "Most accessed a poison that can be easily imported and that, because of weakened regulation, remains readily available." They asked for an urgent meeting with the Prime Minister to discuss their concerns.

Molly Rose Foundation demands swift sanctions after Ofcom update on suicide forum READ MORE :

View 2 Images David Parfett's son Tom was aged just 22-years-old when he took his own life (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

Ofcom fined the forum's provider £950,000 in May for failing to comply with duties under the Online Safety Act. The media regulator said it had found that illegal suicide content is present on the forum.

‌



This included instructional "guides" and threads detailing different methods of suicide, some of which have been present on the site for years. Ofcom has blocked access to the site for the "vast majority" of UK users.

But the online forum - which the Mirror has chosen not to name - can still be accessed by people in the UK using a Virtual Private Network (VPN), a security tool which obscures a user's location. Ofcom in July admitted it is unable to take further legal action against the forum.

The MRF criticised the conclusion as denying "justice and accountability" to bereaved families. The charity also criticised a decision by prosecutors not to try to extradite Kenneth Law, a Canadian who used the forum to sell poison to at least 79 UK, to face charges in the UK.

‌



The letter to Mr Burnham outlined concerns that Prevention of Future Deaths reports raised relevant matters of concern 43 times, while coroners raised concerns about either the substance or the forum with public bodies some 65 times. It added: "Why were so many opportunities missed while people continued to die and suffer harm?" The letter also criticised Ofcom for being unwilling or unable to act with the urgency that was so desperately required".

Bereaved families and the survivor likened their experience with the state to that of the victims of Grenfell, the infected blood sandal, the post office scandal, and Hillsborough families, who were "each denied justice, accountability and dignity because governments and public bodies repeatedly chose to close ranks".

The letter continued: "We write to you today as a group of bereaved families and a survivor of an appalling suicide grooming forum that exists for only one purpose: To groom, coerce and instruct vulnerable people to take their own lives, and to celebrate when those live send.

‌



"Multiple agencies have failed to act and we live with the consequences of those failures every day. We demand a full public inquiry; nothing less will honour our children, the survivors, or expose the failures that cost their lives."

It added: “The deaths of each of our loved ones were only the start of the continuous trauma we have been left to endure. We must not only bear the pain of their loss but the agony of knowing that their deaths were preventable. They were victims not only of a deadly forum and nihilistic criminals, but also the failure of successive governments that acted too slowly to heed warnings - if at all."

In September last year, David Parfett, whose 22-year-old son Tom took his own life in 2021 and who has signed the letter to Mr Burnham, told The Mirror: “I know from my own personal experience having ordered it three times now that it still gets through to people. It’s a scandal that we’re letting people still take their own lives...

‌



“The saddest thing is always, even as we sit here today, four years after Tom died, that’s still happening today. There are still children and young adults being influenced to die using exactly the same pattern as Tom. And it needs to stop."

Families and campaigners last year called on Keir Starmer to launch an inquiry, but their demands came to no avail.

Andy Burrows, MRF's chief executive, said: “In the past year, every meaningful avenue for justice has been systematically closed off to bereaved families. The State’s failures have directly contributed to the sheer scale of preventable harm we’ve seen, despite a flurry of warnings from families and survivors, as well as multiple coroners across the country.

‌



“The evidence is undeniable, and yet this criminal, nihilistic and financially motivated suicide grooming forum is still active and directly responsible for appalling loss of life here in the UK. Andy Burnham was unflinching in his commitment to the Hillsborough families to seek justice and accountability. He must do the same for these families and survivors, making sure lessons are learned and that families are afforded the same sense of dignity and a commitment the Government is determined to finally make things right.”

An Ofcom spokesman said: “We acted quickly against this forum as soon as the Online Safety Act came into force and have used the powers we’ve been granted to the fullest extent possible. We conducted a thorough investigation under the process required by law and issued a significant fine for breaches of the Act.

“We can only apply for a court order to block a site in the UK if there is ongoing non-compliance under the Act. The forum has already blocked the UK as a direct result of our action, which will better protect people in the UK and means all possible legal routes under the Act have now been exhausted."

Article continues below

Ofcom has no role in launching a public inquiry – this can only be done by Government. A Government spokesperson said: "We have met with many bereaved families affected by these issues and know nothing can undo the pain they have suffered.

"It is illegal to encourage and assist suicide or serious self-harm online, and sites promoting this content will face the full force of the law.

"Ofcom’s enforcement action has resulted in the forum blocking access to people in the UK, and we will continue to work with law enforcement partners to intercept harmful substances entering our nation."

News.title: Couple jailed over ‘depraved’ plans to sexually abuse young girl in Wales
News.content:
Couple jailed over ‘depraved’ plans to sexually abuse young girl in Wales

Victoria and Shaun Lewis, both 40, have been jailed after planning to sexually abuse a young girl in what has been described as a 'particularly depraved' case

View Image Victoria Lewis and Shaun Lewis have both been jailed (Image: South Wales Police)

A couple has been jailed after making "depraved" plans to sexually exploit a teenage girl.

Victoria Lewis, 40, arranged for the girl to meet her partner, Shaun Lewis, also 40, knowing he would sexually exploit her. The woman also arranged for an indecent photograph to be taken of the child and for her to travel to an area where the abuse would take place.

Shaun Lewis, from Sandfields in Port Talbot, made "numerous sexual requests and demands" of the victim directly to her and also through Victoria Lewis. Detective constable Amanda Jenkins, of South Wales Police, described what the Neath Port Talbot couple put the child through as "horrifying".

DC Jenkins said: "This has been a particularly depraved case which has involved Victoria Lewis arranging for a child to meet with a man she knew would sexually exploit her. What Victoria Lewis has done is sickening and to think about what the child has gone through because of Victoria Lewis is horrifying.

Moment man drives on wrong side during police chase before running into A-road READ MORE :

"We cannot praise the victim enough for the bravery she has shown to tell police what happened to her and secure justice against a despicable woman – and that is before even mentioning Shaun Lewis’ part in the offending."

Victoria Lewis, from Neath, pleaded not guilty to arranging the sexual exploitation of a child aged 13 to 17, arranging sexual activity with a child, and arranging travel with a view to exploitation.

She was found guilty of all three charges following a trial in April and sentenced to four years in prison, Wales Online reports.

Shaun Lewis pleaded guilty to arranging the sexual exploitation of a child, arranging a child sexual offence, and arranging travel with a view to exploitation.

He was handed an extended sentence of 12 years comprising seven years in prison and a licence period of five years.

A South Wales Police spokesman said: "We never underestimate how difficult it is for survivors of sexual abuse to speak out and report.

"But we hope cases like this one provide reassurance that victims will be listened to, treated with dignity and respect, and will be supported throughout the judicial process.

"If you have been sexually abused, and you are not yet ready to report to police, please don’t suffer in silence." Both defendants will have notification requirements for life.

News.title: 'Earl Spencer's memoir strikes at the King but will also plunge dagger into Diana's sons' hearts'
News.content:
The devastating manner in which Diana, Princess of Wales was tragically killed, opened wounds for her loved ones that will never heal.

For her two sons, just 15 and 12 at the time their mother was cruelly and catastrophically taken from them, it has shaped almost every facet of their life since then.

William and Harry have frequently spoken of their lifelong desire to honour her legacy, in their charity work, their roles in public life and indeed after having families of their own, to keep her spirit alive.

How shattering it must be then, to have her memory excavated in such wounding detail. The content of Diana’s brother, Earl Spencer's memoir, not only strikes at the heart of the monarchy, with his lethal character assassination of King Charles, and the wild allegations of his reaction to his ex-wife’s death, but plunges a dagger into the heart of Diana’s beloved sons.

‌



View 3 Images Diana, Princess of Wales, died nearly 30 years ago (Image: WireImage)

It is without question that despite their differences since Harry decided to walk away from his royal role, of which Diana would no doubt have been disturbed over had she lived to see them as men, husbands and fathers, both William and Harry will be deeply disturbed over their uncle’s claims.

Spencer’s claims of the then Prince Charles not only suggesting he - and the royal family - would “forget her soon enough”, and that he was “giddily elated” and sounded like a “lottery winner” when he called him after Diana’s death, are harmful on multiple counts.

Of course, if taken at face value, they threaten not only public perception of the King, who has undergone three decades of carefully cultivated image repair, but could also could have devastating consequences for his relationship with his children.

‌



View 3 Images Earl Charles Spencer has penned a bombshell new book (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

William and Harry have in the past been incredibly open about their father’s misgivings. He was of course the polar opposite parent in many ways to Diana. A product of his own cold upbringing in an unforgiving institution that is not without fault. But what they do acknowledge is after being plunged into becoming a single parent, aside from burying himself in work, he did at least try to shield them from more heartache as best he could in those immediate years following their mother’s passing.

Whereas Harry has used his exit from the monarchy to criticise his family and lay the blame at them for his mental health issues when he was at his most vulnerable, William is an entirely different man. He believes in actions and not words to fulfil his duties as a father and a future king, and will be devastated that his mother’s legacy is being talked about in such terms as we approach the 30th anniversary of her death.

Whether Earl Spencer has any regard for that is a matter for him. What is undeniable is that the King and his heir are united on many matters concerning the business of the family playing out in public and after the monarch's stinging rebuke of Spencer’s claims, in that grief may have clouded his judgement in such recollections, they will unanimous in their despair at this latest war of words.

News.title: Sixth train operator - Chiltern Railways - to go into public ownership in days - what it means for you
News.content:
Sixth train operator - Chiltern Railways - to go into public ownership in days - what it means for you

Chiltern Railways will be the latest operator to become publicly owned at the weekend, with the Department for Transport (DfT) promising extra services, more seats and less overcrowding

View 2 Images Chiltern Railways will come under public ownership on Sunday (Image: Getty)

A railway operator connecting London with the West Midlands will become the sixth to transfer into public ownership on Sunday.

‌



Chiltern Railways will see an extra 25 daily services added from December to tackle chronic overcrowding, the Department for Transport (DfT) vowed. Rail Minister Lord Hendy said the move, which was confirmed in May, will give passengers more frequent and comfortable trains which turn up on time.

‌



Improvements will mean 10,000 additional seats every weekday, the DfT said. Chiltern follows South Western Railway, c2c, Greater Anglia, West Midlands Trains and Govia Thameslink into public ownership.

‌



Labour came to power pledging to set up a new national operator, Great British Railways (GBR), promising a new era of improved public transport. Lord Hendy said: "Every transfer into public ownership gives us the chance to tackle the bread-and-butter issues people care about – more frequent, comfortable trains that turn up on time.

"As we set up Great British Railways, we’re putting passengers first. It will not happen overnight, but we will build a railway the country can trust and rely on and that will create growth, jobs and homes."

View 2 Images Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander ahead of Govia Thameslink being brought into public ownership this year (Image: Getty Images)

‌



In a statement the DfT said the 25 extra weekday services will include half hourly trains on the Chiltern Mainline between London and Birmingham. There will also be six state-of-the-art Chiltern Explorer trains in operation from December, with better air-conditioning and wi-fi.

And the government has pledged all carriages will be improved by 2028, with charging points at every seat after a £12million refurbishment. There will also be improvements at stations, including more parking spaces at Haddenham and Thame Parkway, it said.

Tony Baxter, interim managing director of Chiltern Railways, said: "Sunday is a significant milestone for Chiltern Railways and we look forward to working together with the wider rail industry to deliver a better railway for everyone in Great Britain.

Article continues below

"Over the next 12 months, our customers in London, Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire, Warwickshire and the West Midlands will benefit from more new trains, more services, thousands of additional seats, improvements to stations and on-board facilities and the ability to use their ticket on other operators when faced with disruption – customer improvements made possible thanks to years of planning, dedication and hard work by Chiltern colleagues."

On December 13 Great Western Railway will become the seventh to become publicly owned, with all operators set to be in public hands by the end of 2027.

The government says bringing track and train services under one organisation will make the network more efficient and result in problems being fixed faster.

News.title: Remains found after wildfire identified as mother-of-three missing since 2019
News.content:
Human remains discovered in woodland in south-west London following a wildfire have been identified as a woman who has been missing since 2019.

Mother-of-three Joanne Sheen, then aged 44, was last seen when she travelled from Fareham to Southampton with a friend on 5 December 2019.

Metropolitan Police officers were called to Padstow Walk in Feltham on 12 August after bones were discovered in an area of shrubland damaged by a fire the previous week.

A 56-year-old man from Southampton has been arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder and he remains in police custody.

Detectives in London have now handed the investigation over to Hampshire Police after the remains were identified as those of Sheen.

Sheen's disappearance sparked a major police investigation, which the force described as "long and complex".

News.title: Charles 'sounded giddily elated' after Diana died, Earl Spencer claims
News.content:
Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, has claimed King Charles "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after her death in 1997.

In a controversial book about Diana, he alleged the then-Prince Charles sounded like a "lottery winner" after the news.

Buckingham Palace strongly pushed back on Wednesday against the credibility of the book, after an initial extract claimed Charles had said of Diana: "We'll forget her soon enough."

A spokesperson said: "While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss."

The latest claims are once again highly personal in their attacks on King Charles and the royals, interpreting their motives in a very harsh light.

The evidence is Earl Spencer's own recollection of conversations about that emotional time around his sister's death, almost 30 years ago.

What remains to be seen is how the public might respond to the allegations, whether they might support this book as a new and different Spencer perspective, or whether they might feel it to be inappropriate to be sharing such private disputes.

Representatives of Prince Harry have said they do not want to comment on the book and Buckingham Palace has pointed back to its response from Wednesday, when it rejected the account of Prince Charles in the wake of Diana's death in Paris.

News.title: Interest rates held but Bank signals rise if energy prices stay high
News.content:
The Bank of England has held interest rates at their current rate of 3.75% for the sixth time in a row but said they were likely to rise if high energy prices persist.

The US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted global energy supplies leading to a sharp increase in petrol and diesel prices and an uptick in inflation.

But Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said energy price volatility made it more likely that interest rates would rise.

The Bank also announced it was slowing its sales of UK government debt, prompting an easing in the UK's long-term borrowing costs.

The Bank of England's main interest rate is a crucial benchmark for banks and other lenders in setting interest rates for individuals and businesses who want to borrow or save money. Higher rates can help dampen inflationary pressures, while lower rates can help boost spending and investment.

The UK's central bank aims to keep inflation at a target of 2%, but it has been above that rate for nearly two years, with inflation hitting 3.1% in August.

On Thursday the Bank of England raised its forecast for inflation predicting it would be "slightly above 4%" at the start of next year. It warned that the price cap on household gas and electricity bills for January was "now expected to rise substantially further".

Speaking after the Bank's decision, Bailey said the direct impact of higher energy prices was clear, but officials were still assessing how far those costs would feed through into wider inflation across the economy.

News.title: Father's tribute to 'sweetest little boy' Noah Woods
News.content:
People from as far afield as Birmingham and Hampshire turned up to help with the search for Noah, who was from nearby East Bergholt.

Helicopters, dog units and members of the public had been scouring the area, close to the River Stour on the Suffolk-Essex border.

Reflecting on the community response, Woods wrote in his Facebook post: "It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation.

"You have all taken Noah into your own hearts, with all the overwhelming help, we were all just trying to bring him home to us safe and sound."

He thanked everyone who came together to search for "our boy" - listing emergency services, businesses and venues in the village - and "all of the people who gave up their time in their busy schedules to help us when we most needed it".

"The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives."

He finished the post by addressing his son.

"It has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short three years you were with us."

Suffolk Police said his death was not being treated as suspicious, but that officers still had inquiries to complete before submitting a file for the coroner.

Supt Tom Pearse thanked the family for their "patience and understanding throughout the searches".

"It was clear from the media coverage we saw that they not only had all of Suffolk behind them, but an outpouring of goodwill from across the entire country and beyond.

"I know how grateful Noah's family are for all the support and kind messages they have received, but would reiterate our plea to now allow them the time, space and privacy they need at this deeply distressing time."

News.title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
News.content:
King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.

Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.

It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.

The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.

News.title: Archbishop of Canterbury withdraws award from Muslim cleric who praised Osama bin Laden
News.content:
The Archbishop of Canterbury has withdrawn an award given to a Muslim cleric who praised Osama Bin Laden.

Hafiz Muhammad Tahir Mehmood Ashrafi received the award for reconciliation and interfaith cooperation from Dame Sarah Mullally last week, on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.

Lambeth Palace faced a backlash after it emerged Ashrafi praised Bin Laden - the architect of the 2001 attacks - as someone who had "been fighting for Islam against the Russians, Americans and British", in comments from 2007.

Ashrafi also reportedly said he would give Bin Laden the title Saifullah, which means "Sword of God". He told the BBC his remarks had been "totally taken out of context".

Lambeth Palace now says "comments made by Imam Ashrafi have come to light that have led (us) to reconsider this award and we can now confirm that the award has been withdrawn".

In presenting the award last week, the Archbishop's office said Ashrafi was being honoured for "his outstanding work as an ambassador of interfaith harmony in Pakistan, known for his commitment to promoting religious tolerance".

His award was presented by Dame Sarah in a ceremony that coincided with the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in the US in which nearly 3,000 people were killed.

Ashrafi told the BBC that his remarks had been "totally taken out of context" and the backlash had been "an unfair campaign" against him.

He said that he was only speaking about Bin Laden in 2007 in response to "the hurt felt by many Muslims" over a knighthood being awarded to the Satanic Verses author Sir Salman Rushdie.

But he defended the comparison he made between an author and a man who was behind the deaths of thousands of people.

Criticism of Ashrafi has gone beyond his comments about Bin Laden.

In giving him his award for promoting interfaith harmony last week, Lambeth Palace had cited the fact that Ashrafi had intervened in the 2012 case of Rimsha Masih, a young Christian girl in Pakistan falsely accused of blasphemy.

But Ashrafi has otherwise been supportive of Pakistan's blasphemy laws that have led to an estimated 2000 people being prosecuted since the late 1980s.

They include a disproportionately high number of Pakistan's minority Christians and Ahmadis in particular, but many majority Sunni Muslims too.

Ashrafi claimed the blasphemy laws actually "save lives", stopping people taking matters into their own hands.

But Human Rights Watch said last year that "the laws perpetuate religious discrimination and are used to target the poor and minorities in unlawful evictions and land grabs".

The organisation has called on the Pakistani government to urgently reform the laws to prevent them "being weaponised to [...] attack marginalised communities".

News.title: Watch: Can humpback whales experience grief?
News.content:
Humpback whale mothers may experience grief when their calves die, a rare observation led by Griffith University and Sea World Foundation has found.

The BBC's Tiffanie Turnbull explains everything you need to know about the sighting off Australia's Gold Coast, and why it's so rare.

News.title: Ed Sheeran's tour in 'damage control mode' after Macklemore backlash
News.content:
Robert Kraft, the US stadium owner who had pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore removed as Ed Sheeran's opening act, says Sheeran asked him to match his own $2m (Â£1.5m) donation for "aid in the region".

It came after Macklemore said he would donate $1m (Â£750,000) to Palestinian organisations, challenging Kraft to match him.

Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots, wrote on Wednesday: "Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis.

"Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges."

The BBC's Mark Savage looks at the controversy over Sheeran's US tour and why it is in "damage control mode".

News.title: Healey to ask EU finance ministers to let UK into 'Made in Europe' industry scheme
News.content:
The chancellor is to warn the European Union (EU) not to lock the UK out of its scheme to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

John Healey will push for closer UK-EU partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday.

But he will call on the EU to design its "Made in Europe" programme in a way that deepens ties with the UK "rather than erecting new barriers", Treasury sources told the BBC.

Officials said Healey will tell European finance ministers it is important to "learn lessons" after talks collapsed last year for Britain to join an EU defence loans scheme.

That dispute centred on how much money the UK would pay to join.

The "Made in Europe" policy, officially called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), is currently being considered by the bloc and aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries.

There is concern in government the scheme could lock British firms out of European supply chains.

Treasury officials said Healey wanted to reduce the economic impact of Brexit and build closer ties with the EU, but not at any cost to the UK.

Healey said: "The next chapter of Britain's growth story will be written in more places.

"To me, closer ties with the EU means British businesses â wherever they are based across the UK â get better access to both the supply chains and the customers they need to grow."

Healey will use the meeting in Dublin to focus on tech firms, defence companies, and manufacturing.

"The chancellor wants to make sure nothing holds them back," a Treasury source said.

It comes after a reset summit with the EU was delayed after Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister.

Treasury sources now expect that to take place in November.

Healey's meeting in Dublin comes after it emerged earlier this week that he is in discussions about joining a global investment bank aimed at raising more money for defence spending.

He is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea.

Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending.

Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review.

News.title: UK Youth Parliament looks set to be axed
News.content:
The UK Youth Parliament is at risk of being axed within months, BBC News has learned, as the government is not committing to funding it any longer.

The parliament was launched in 2000 to boost interest in politics among young people and has more than 300 elected members aged between 11 and 18.

Once a year, the young politicians are allowed to hold debates in the House of Commons chamber, on a day when MPs are not sitting.

Some MPs and young people say axing it would be a blow for youth democracy, while others say it is not providing value for money.

The Department of Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS), which funds the parliament each year with taxpayer cash, is not committing to giving any more grants to it.

A spokesperson for the DCMS praised the youth parliament's "important legacy... giving elected young people a national platform to represent their peers, engage with decision-makers and develop confidence, leadership and skills for life and work".

It received Â£453,000 in taxpayer funding in the last year alone with about Â£2.4m public money spent on it among other youth initiatives between 2017 and 2024.

While no final decision has been made on funding beyond March 2027, a government source said: "The government has not committed to continuing the programme in its current form."

UK Youth Parliament insiders told the BBC that without government funding, it is likely to close.

It follows a government review, external published in October last year, which concluded that while the parliament was delivering on its intended goals, only a quarter of young people know about it - and some schools felt "excluded from the process".

The government says it is working with young people and youth organisations to design a new scheme that increases their involvement in democracy and decision-making, with further announcements to be made this autumn.

Any new scheme will have a "particular focus on under-represented groups", a government source said.

Bobby Forbes, the recently departed chair of the UK Youth Parliament's Youth Select Committee, which works with officials in Westminster, said it gives teenagers "a direct way to scrutinise government and hold decision-makers to account".

News.title: Andy Burnham urged to set dementia waiting-time target
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is facing calls to set a national waiting-time target for dementia care in England.

An Alzheimer's Society proposal to set an 18âweek referralâtoâtreatment target has been backed by Professor Sir Mike Richards, England's former national cancer director, and Baroness Louise Casey, who's leading a major review of adult social care.

In a report, Alzheimer's Society and the King's Trust said a "cancer-style revolution" was needed to improve dementia care, which they described as being "stuck in the 20th century".

In a speech at Alzheimer's Society conference on Thursday, Social Care Minister Alison McGovern expressed support for the report, external.

She said: "The report that the Alzheimer's Society published today on going on the journey that we've been on with cancer, with Alzheimer's and dementia, I think that's spot on."

The minister said dementia had been "neglected for far too long".

She added: "And nowhere is this division between health and social care felt more sharply than by people living with dementia in their families, too often left to navigate a shattered system at the most difficult time in their lives."

The government has committed to appointing a top official to oversee dementia care and publish a new plan - a modern service framework - to speed up support for those with the disease by the end of the year.

McGovern said the government would "appoint a dementia tsar, backed with real expertise".

Currently there is no waiting-time target for dementia in England.

In contrast, the NHS sets waiting-time targets for cancer diagnosis and treatment.

Professor Richards was the national cancer director when these cancer targets were introduced in 2000, and said he thought an 18âweek referralâtoâtreatment target for dementia patients was achievable.

He said setting such a target would require "political initiative" and extra funding.

"All of that is going to cost more money but remember the toll that this condition is taking at the moment, both on the people affected by dementia themselves and their relatives," the professor said.

The same proposal has been made by Baroness Casey.

In a letter to former Health Secretary Wes Streeting in March, she said the government should look at "how dementia can be put on a level playing field with other conditions, for example by setting national standards for dementia diagnosis, including an 18âweek referralâtoâtreatment target".

Speaking to the BBC, Baroness Casey said she agreed with the proposal to emulate cancer care.

She said: "I think the National Health Service and more generally all of us have stuck our heads in the sand about it, and it's time we started saying, yes, we should have a similar mission, and we should do as much as we possibly can on dementia, and now."

Baroness Casey is expected to publish her recommendations on social care reform next summer.

About one million people are living with dementia in the UK, a figure expected to reach 1.4 million by 2040.

Burnham cancelled his engagements earlier this week after the death of father, Roy, who had Alzheimer's disease.

Returning from compassionate leave, he said his father would have wanted him "back out there" to bring forward "the changes that he always pushed me to make".

In July, Burnham spoke about his father's condition and said it had influenced his drive to reform adult social care in England.

Burnham has said he will wait for Baroness Casey's recommendations before deciding what changes to make to social care and how it's funded.

News.title: UK needs 'credible path' on defence spending, says Nato chief
News.content:
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said he is confident the UK government understands the need for a "credible path" to increase defence spending.

The alliance's secretary general told the BBC he was "absolutely confident" in the UK's commitment to hit a Nato-wide spending target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035.

Speaking after meetings in London, he said British ministers accepted the need to make yearly steps towards hitting the target.

But he accepted that the exact "pathway" towards the goal would not be set out until next year.

Andy Burnham has followed predecessor Sir Keir Starmer in committing to reach Nato's 3.5% spending target by 2035, up from an estimated 2.6% this year.

He has said date for reaching a planned 3% interim target will come next spring, when the long-term budgets of government departments are due to be set.

But he has faced pressure to immediately commit to reaching the milestone by the end of the decade. His chancellor and ex-defence secretary John Healey has previously argued this would show Britain was serious about the Nato goal.

Former Dutch PM Rutte has been encouraging members of the alliance not to pencil in large spending increases shortly before the deadline.

Speaking to BBC political editor Chris Mason after meeting Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in London, Rutte said he was confident British ministers understood the 2035 target could not be met "in one go in 2034".

"I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the 3.5[%] they are there," he said.

"I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the yearly increments, they totally take it and accept it, that they have to be there.

"There has to be a credible path. What that credible path exactly will be, we will see with the spending review next year," he added.

News.title: Man, 29, jailed for raping two 14-year-old girls
News.content:
A man has been jailed for 14 years for raping two teenage girls after encouraging them to drink alcohol at his flat.

Sultani Bakatash, 29, an Afghan, met one of the girls on Snapchat before inviting her and her friend to his home in Georgina Court, Bolton, Greater Manchester, on 6 December.

Bolton Crown Court heard the 14-year-old girls drank vodka and Coke and became so intoxicated they were passing in and out of consciousness before Bakatash raped and sexually assaulted them.

Following a four-week trial, he was convicted of two counts of rape, one of sexual assault and one of assault by penetration. The judge said his work with the British Army in Afghanistan might mean he was not deported.

One of the girls managed to escape from the flat and knocked on a neighbour's door, the court heard.

She said: "He's trying to rape my friend. She's locked in. He's raping her."

The court heard Bakatash encouraged the girls to keep drinking while taking only a sip himself and complimenting them on their appearance.

Charlotte Rimmer, prosecuting, said he had arranged to meet the girls, encouraged them to drink and then seized the opportunity to rape them.

She described him as "a man, intent on sexual gratification, regardless of what they wanted".

The court heard both girls became so drunk they passed out and each witnessed the other being raped and sexually assaulted.

News.title: Ukrainian guilty of vandalism at mosques linked to Russian network behind Starmer arson attack
News.content:
A Ukrainian man has pleaded guilty to spraying abusive graffiti on mosques in east London, in a case linked to the Russian state network behind arson attacks against the former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

Illia Bilyk, 21, entered guilty pleas at Thames Magistrates' Court to five counts of racially and religiously aggravated criminal damage.

Bilyk sprayed graffiti on the Stratford Islamic Association, Al-Birr Mosque and Leyton Jamia Masjid on 23 January 2025. Two days later he targeted Noor Ul Islam Primary School and the Islamic Shariah Council.

The BBC has learned that Bilyk told police he was recruited into spraying the graffiti by a Russian speaker after being approached on the messaging app Telegram.

Bilyk said the Russian speaker told him where to target and paid him afterwards.

In June this year two Ukrainians - Roman Lavrynovych and Stanislav Carpiuc - were jailed for conspiring to carry out arson attacks targeting a property and a car connected to prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

An investigation by the BBC and Hope not Hate revealed that Russia was behind the arson attacks and had also generated Islamophobic vandalism throughout London, including on the east London venues which Biluyk has now admitted vandalising.

News.title: RNLI station out-of-service after anti-migrant protests
News.content:
Portsmouth's lifeboat station remains temporarily out of service following anti-migrant protests.

Protesters blocked roads in the city on 6 September after about 120 people arrived at the Eastney Landing ferry port area following a Channel small boat crossing. The RNLI helped bring them ashore.

The RNLI also said it helped to ensure the safety of anti-migrant demonstrators who went into the sea.

Following the protest, the charity's chief executive said staff had faced "unacceptable" online and physical abuse. The lifeboat station was taken out of service on 10 September, meanwhile, abuse aimed at volunteers also forced the lifeboat museum in Poole to shut for several days.

The RNLI said: "Search and rescue cover continues to be provided through established contingency arrangements, including flank RNLI stations and other declared assets.

"We hope to have the lifeboat station back on service as soon as possible."

After abuse was directed at its crews tasked to assist the incident, its chief executive issued a statement.

Peter Sparkes said: "Recent events have generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding about the RNLI â our purpose, our tasking, and particularly our lifesaving work in the Channel.

"Sadly, as a result, some of our volunteers and staff have been the subject of online and, in the worst cases, physical abuse.

"The RNLI's people represent the very best in our society, they selflessly give up their time to keep others safe."

He added: "Stand by them, not against them and their families. I am extremely proud of and grateful for their vital lifesaving work."

The protest in Portsmouth followed a separate demonstration the previous day, in which hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters brought the Port of Dover to a standstill.

The protests led the RNLI to also review its security procedures. As part of this, volunteers were told to consider not wearing RNLI-branded clothing in some circumstances while representing the charity.

News.title: Former MI6 spy takes Trump to Scottish court for £800,000 legal payout
News.content:
A company founded by a former spy is pursuing Donald Trump at a small Scottish court for more than Â£800,000 in unpaid legal costs.

The US president was named in a hearing at Ayr Sheriff Court as Orbis Business Intelligence seeks funds from the Trump Turnberry golf resort.

The case concerns legal costs owed by Trump from a 2024 English data protection case against Orbis's director Christopher Steele - a former MI6 agent.

But SLC Turnberry Limited - which owns the course - is disputing Trump's role as the "ultimate owner", arguing that his stake in the course is held by a trust.

Steele was the author of a salacious "dossier" linking Trump to Russia during his 2016 election campaign.

London's High Court of Justice ruled Trump's action out of time and a judge ordered him to pay Orbis Â£680,000 in legal costs.

Orbis is targeting the president's financial interests at Turnberry in order to claim the funds.

The case called at Ayr Sheriff Court because the resort falls within its jurisdiction, while Steele and Orbis have no connections there.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned on Thursday that Russia is planning hybrid strikes with drones or rockets on European countries supporting Ukraine, among them Poland.

Russia will pretend the attacks are “accidental” in order to “paralyze or at least weaken the motivation of NATO countries" to rush to the defense of the member state coming under attack, Tusk said in a speech to the Polish parliament.

“There is a real risk that drones or other types of projectiles will enter the territory of one or several countries on the eastern flank and even cause destruction," Tusk warned.

“The official narration will be that it’s an accident and there is no reason for NATO to think about a response,” he added.

He said Russia was more dangerous because it was increasingly using jet-powered drones, which fly higher and faster and thus are more difficult to detect by air defense before reaching their targets.

Tusk has been for months warning that Russia might be preparing a more serious hybrid attack against a NATO country. His warnings have gotten increasingly specific as he received intelligence from NATO, Ukrainian and U.S. secret services, including the CIA, he said.

In recent days, Tusk has said Russia was now focusing on attacking border crossings between Ukraine and its European neighbors in order to disrupt delivery lines to Ukraine. Four such incidents happened on Poland's border with Ukraine in the past week and several others took place in the last weeks on Ukraine's border with Moldova.

Tusk said at the moment Russia was not ready for any peace talks “without the total capitulation of Ukraine.”

“They are convinced the winter will be tragically critical for Ukraine,” Tusk said. He said last winter Poland stepped in with deliveries when Ukraine's energy infrastructure came under attack, but if border crossings are destroyed, it will be much harder for Warsaw to offer such help this upcoming winter.

“Russia's goal is to destroy as much as possible the economy and logistics of Ukraine,” Tusk said, adding that intelligence indicates continuous attacks of “very high frequency and intensity” on six main Ukrainian cities should be expected in the near future.

Tusk announced on Thursday he would travel to Ukraine overnight to Friday, in what can be seen as an act of defiance against Russia after European leaders narrowly escaped a drone strike on a train near the Polish-Ukrainian border on Sunday. Officials usually keep their travel plans to Ukraine secret for security reasons.

In Kyiv, he said he would discuss with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy how to defend against the new types of drones as well as discuss with partners including Slovakia about further sanctions against Russia.

On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that “major progress is being made toward establishing a U.S. Army base in Poland” after a U.S. delegation was in Poland last week to visit several possible locations.

“If this happens, the location will be announced very soon,” Trump wrote. “This will be a historic step for our Great U.S./Polish Alliance.”

Poland has for years sought to host a permanent U.S. base as a strong guarantee of its security in the face of the rising Russian threat.

Poland’s high defense spending and major U.S. arms purchases have persuaded the Trump administration to consider putting a permanent base in Poland even as it reorganizes and reduces its overall military presence in Europe.

In May, the U.S. unexpectedly withdrew troops from the total of around 10,000 stationed in Poland, causing confusion among European allies and nervousness in Warsaw. But officials in both Poland and the U.S. soon said the withdrawal was temporary and Poland was not expected to suffer from the U.S. troop reorganization.

News.title: William and Kate take swing at Shinty: ‘Try again!’
News.content:
Prince William and Princess Kate met dozens of residents on Scotland’s Isle of Bute, posed for selfies and even played shinty as they celebrated the island’s community spirit and volunteering ethos

After watching an under 17s match from the sidelines with many locals on Thursday (17 September), the couple tried playing the sport and quickly learned hand-eye co-ordination was key as they practiced taking penalties.

William fluffed his first shot with the ball moving just a few inches before making solid contact to cheers from the spectators.

Kate fared little better at the start, swinging and missing but her next shot was cheered as it flew at the goalkeeper and she peppered the goal with more shots, almost hitting press closest to the netting .

City officials in Southlake, Texas, have denied a Pride festival a permit to hold an event scheduled for this October despite granting the same permit last year, according to local reports.

On Tuesday, the Southlake City Council voted to deny Pride Kel-So festival organizers a permit they are seeking for an October event, according to Fox 4.

Only two people spoke about the event during the city council meeting, with one person speaking in favor of the event and another speaking in opposition to the festival. None of the city councilors offered comment or asked the organizers any questions.

The council issued a unanimous vote against the permit. Now, the organizers are seeking an explanation.

"I am just in shock still," April Dreyson, one of the festival's co-founders, told the outlet. She said that the city council has not explained its vote despite approving the festival a year prior.

St. Martin-in-the-Fields Episcopal Church in Southlake, Texas. The church was meant to be the site of the Pride Kel-So festival in October, but the Southlake City Council denied the group a permit for the event despite approving the event the year prior ( Google )

According to the festival's organizers, the inaugural Pride Kel-So festival was approved in 2025. It was held at St. Martin-in-the-Fields Episcopal Church in Southlake. The name "Kel-So" is a combination of the words Keller and Southlake, referencing the fact that the church that hosted the festival sits on the border of the two cities.

They told Fox 4 that 2,500 people attended the event, which they described as family-friendly. The festival, which celebrates the LGBT community, featured live music and vendors.

"We followed all the recommendations and did not expect, especially with no comments, no questions. If they had concerns, they didn’t bring them up," Dreyson said.

In a Facebook post after the vote, Dreyson said the only explanation for the denial she could think of is discrimination.

“There is no explanation for the city council's vote other than pure discrimination against a group of people. Zero excuse," she wrote.

The individual who spoke in support of the event was the church's associate pastor, Reverend Ellen Singer.

"It’s clear there is conflict. It’s clear there is some sort of rupture in the community and actually the goal of something like this is to bring people together, to celebrate being a community with one another," she told Fox 4.

The church's leader, Reverend Alan Bentrup, told the Fort Worth Star-Telegram that he was out of town at the time of the council meeting, but that he supports the festival and wants to host it again this year.

“We’ve been clear from the beginning that we want to [host the Pride Kel-So event]. We are willing and eager to host whatever might be possible,” Bentrup said.

The opposing voice at the city council meeting said that the festival was "abhorrent" and drew protesters to the event.

Bentrup said he had been to numerous "contentious" city council meetings and noted that it was unusual that one dissenting voice would sway the council's vote.

“One person speaking against doesn’t usually fit that,” he said.

If the council does not reconsider, the festival organizers said it could downsize the festival and limit the number of guests to 1,000 people. Any gathering of 1,000 people or more requires a permit per the city's laws.

Dreyson told Fox 4 that she and the other festival organizers would "figure it out," and has been adamant on social media that the festival will happen in one form or another.

Pilar Schank, a spokesperson for the city, declined to comment on the matter and directed The Independent to a video of the September 15 city council meeting.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva signed a decree on Thursday increasing benefits under his flagship welfare program by 15%, weeks before the first round of the presidential elections.

The minimum monthly benefit per family of Bolsa Familia, or Family Grant, will rise to 691 reais ($134) next month, from 600 reais ($117). The decree says that it adjusts payments for accumulated inflation since March 2023.

The measure will increase the purchasing power of some voters, who will decide in October whether to grant Lula a fourth, nonconsecutive term, or elect Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, a son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, in a likely run-off vote. Polls show the two are currently running neck-and-neck.

“Bolsa Familia is central to our strategy to look after more vulnerable families, guarantee income so that people emerge from poverty and don’t suffer from food insecurity,” Finance Minister Dario Durigan said.

The additional spending would be absorbed within existing budget allocations and would not represent a new expenditure, he added.

The measure will cost 5.8 billion reais ($1.1 billion) this year and around 22 billion reais ($4.3 billion) next year, a statement from the Brazilian government's communications secretariat said. The average benefit will increase from 675 reais ($132) to 777 reais ($151), the statement added.

Millions of families will receive the new amount from Oct. 19. The potential run-off vote is scheduled for Oct. 25.

The announcement prompted lawmaker and Sen. Bolsonaro ally Marcos Antônio Pereira Gomes, known as Zé Trovão, to ask Brazil's electoral court to suspend the decree, alleging that it amounts to an electoral measure that violates Brazilian law, according to local press articles shared by Trovão on social media.

Some justices from Brazil’s top court also sit on the country’s electoral court. Supreme Court Justice André Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee who faces accusations of political bias, was appointed to oversee the case brought by Trovão, local press reported.

Late on Thursday, Mendonca dismissed the case without considering its merits, ruling that Trovão lacked standing to file the complaint, local press said.

Lula introduced the cash-transfer program at the beginning of his first term in 2003. It provides financial aid to low-income families, conditional on children’s school attendance and health requirements, such as vaccinations.

Bolsa Familia was the subject of thousands of academic studies in Brazil and abroad, which reported significant reductions in poverty, inequality and infant mortality. Researchers also found greater access to basic health and said school attendance also improved.

Bolsonaro replaced the program with Auxilio Brasil, or Brazil Aid, ahead of the 2022 vote, in what analysts widely saw as an effort to rebrand the popular program associated with Lula to buoy his reelection chances. Lula defeated Bolsonaro.

Last week, Lula signed a decree and a provisional measure aimed at lowering fuel prices, as the U.S.-Iran war drives up the cost of filling the tank. The cost of fuel is a particularly sensitive issue for voters.

Ferencvaros piled on the misery for Celtic with a 3-1 win in their Europa League opener at Parkhead.

Sunday’s bruising 3-0 Scottish League Cup defeat to Rangers had stunned Martin O’Neill’s side, who fell behind in the 20th minute when winger Bamidele Yusuf’s shot deflected off defender Liam Scales and into the net.

Midfielder Mika Baur swept in an equaliser in the 44th minute but before the half-time whistle blew, captain Kristoffer Zachariassen restored the Hungarian side’s lead.

Former Celtic forward Daniel Arzani fired in a stunning 20-yard drive in the 47th minute and Balazs Borbely’s side comfortably kept their lead intact.

O’Neill shuffled his side, with Viljami Sinisalo replacing on-loan goalkeeper Sam Johnstone who had looked shaky in Govan.

Record signing Kasper Hogh was dropped for striker Camilo Duran to move in from the wing, with wide men James Forrest and Haissem Hassan coming in along with midfielder Oliver Sorensen.

open image in gallery Celtic lost again after a disappointing display ( PA )

The visitors started sprightly, Yusuf brilliantly blocking a goal-bound shot from Forrest, and there were a couple of near misses from Duran and Forrest, again.

In the 18th minute, Zachariassen headed a Yusuf cross over the crossbar to hint at the danger to come and two minutes later, when the Nigerian decided to shoot from the edge of the Hoops penalty area, the ball was inadvertently redirected by Scales past the stranded Sinisalo.

Sinisalo dived smartly down to his right to push away a shot from Zachariassen for a 23rd-minute corner which came to nothing, and then a dangerous cross bounced off Mariano Gomez into the arms of the Celtic keeper.

In response, a drive from Celtic captain Callum McGregor was deflected wide for another Hoops corner which proved fruitless.

open image in gallery Celtic managed to pull themselves together towards the end of the first half ( PA )

The home side did level when left-back Kieran Tierney drove into the box and cut the ball back for Baur, handed his first Germany call-up this week, to fire in from 12 yards and it looked like Celtic would have a chance to regroup at the break.

However, in added time, Yusuf dribbled all too easily into the Celtic penalty area and set up Zachariassen to flick the ball in from close range with defenders Scales and Cameron Carter-Vickers in close attendance.

Hogh replaced Sorensen for the start of the second half to go with a front two but before the crowd settled, a Scales mistake ended with Yusuf sending Arzani clear down the left and after turning inside to the edge of the box, he fired high into the top corner.

open image in gallery Martin O’Neill has plenty to ponder ahead of the Old Firm rematch this weekend ( Getty )

Benjamin Nygren and Sebastian Tounekti replaced Forrest and Hassan, soon followed by Luke McCowan, as O’Neill tried another way into a match that was drifting.

Celtic pepped up and in the 69th minute Nygren came close with a curling shot and Tounekti had an effort parried away by keeper Adam Varga, whose mistake allowed Nygren a shot at an empty goal from 30 yards but he missed the target.

It is on to Sunday now for Celtic, who will try to win back the favour of their fed-up fans against their oldest rivals.

A vast majority of voters in key Senate battleground states favor candidates who present explicit plans to reform Social Security over those who pledge to leave the program untouched, according to research conducted by the Peterson Foundation.

The nationwide survey of 2,500 registered voters, conducted between August 20 and August 27, found that more than 80 percent of respondents preferred a representative with a strategy to prevent automatic benefit reductions. In contrast, 17 percent favored candidates promising not to touch the system.

The urgency stems from a tight financial deadline. A report from the Social Security Board of Trustees projected that the trust fund used to top off payroll taxes would run dry in the late months of 2032. If Congress does not intervene before then, the shortfall will force an immediate 22 percent pay cut for all beneficiaries.

Because senators elected this cycle will be in office when the depletion occurs, analysts emphasize that the upcoming elections carry increased weight.

“The voters who will determine the balance of the U. S. Senate are calling on candidates to strengthen the future of Social Security,” Michael Peterson, chief executive of the Peterson Foundation, said. “Senators elected this fall will be in office in 2032 when Social Security recipients will face immediate 22% cuts, so all candidates should be putting forth solutions in this campaign to prevent this catastrophic result.”

open image in gallery Midterm voters in key Senate battleground states strongly favor candidates offering concrete plans to reform Social Security over those who promise to leave the program alone, polling from the Peterson Foundation shows ( Getty Images )

An analysis by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget noted that 63 million Americans — including 54 million retirees and 9 million dependents and survivors — would be affected by the cuts. The average national loss would equal approximately $500 per recipient per month.

In five critical battleground states, the financial burden varies, according to the CRFB analysis.

Texas faces the largest overall hit, where 4.3 million Social Security recipients would see an average monthly reduction of $489.

Ohio follows with 2.2 million residents losing an average of $487 each month, while Michigan has 2 million beneficiaries facing an average monthly loss of $523.

In North Carolina, 2 million people would experience an average monthly decline of $501, and in Georgia, 1.7 million voters face an average monthly drop of $487.

open image in gallery Voters overwhelmingly favor concrete policy changes to secure the program’s future, including a 72 percent approval rating for raising the payroll tax cap on higher incomes ( Getty Images )

The Peterson Foundation survey showed that 91 percent of respondents supported structural reforms once informed of the 2032 automatic cut projections. Additionally, 85 percent indicated that persistent inflation made resolving the funding shortfall urgent.

Survey results showed clear backing for a range of policy changes to keep the program solvent.

Most respondents, 72 percent, favored adding a 1 percent payroll tax on income over $184,500. Two-thirds supported capping annual benefits at $100,000 per retired couple, while 65 percent backed benefit cuts for the top 20 percent of earners. An equal 65 percent favored a combination of gradual benefit changes and tax increases.

“The good news indicated by this survey is that voters want this problem addressed, and there is strong bipartisan support for many available solutions that would sustain this essential program,” Peterson said.

Voters drew a firm line against using national debt to cover the gap. Just 29 percent favored federal borrowing to address the shortfall, while 68 percent explicitly opposed adding to the $40 trillion national deficit.

Crystal Palace made an impressive start to their debut Europa League campaign by sweeping aside Polish champions Lech Poznan 4-0.

Yeremy Pino, Chris Richards and Jorgen Strand Larsen were on target in the first half before Eddie Nketiah fired a late fourth as Palace defied their disappointing Premier League form on a comfortable night at Selhurst Park.

Lech finished with 10 men after Radoslaw Murawski was sent off for a reckless bodycheck on Jaydee Canvot and moments later Nketiah put the finishing touch to a conclusive win.

Palace’s first appearance in the Europa League came a year after they were kicked out of the competition due to a breach of multi-club ownership rules, with Uefa demoting them to the Conference League.

They duly won that, thereby securing their return to the Europa League, and they continued to show theie taste for continental action against opponents who have made a strong start to their Polish title defence.

Boss Pierre Sage named an unchanged team despite Saturday’s 3-2 home defeat by Ipswich and was rewarded by seeing victory wrapped up with just over half an hour on the clock.

open image in gallery Yeremy Pino got the ball rolling for Palace ( Getty )

open image in gallery And the match was over as a contest by half-time ( Reuters )

For all three first-half goals Lech had a hand in their own downfall, the most startling of their errors arriving in the 10th minute when Terry Yegbe sent a throw-in straight to the feet of Pino.

Pino darted between a defence that had been caught by surprise by Yegbe’s blunder before the opportunistic Spanish forward produced a precise finish.

Palace next exploited a static visiting defence when Richards leapt to meet Adam Wharton’s corner at the back post and headed the ball through the hands of goalkeeper Mateusz Lis.

It was all sewn up in the 35th minute through an unstoppable Strand Larsen penalty awarded after Pino had been brought down by Murawski.

open image in gallery Chris Richards produced an unstoppable header ( Reuters )

The hapless Yegbe then unwittingly deflected the ball into his own net from 25 yards amid confusion in the Lech defence, but Strand Larsen was offside and the Ghana centre-back looked skywards in gratitude at being spared responsibility for a second Palace goal.

Lech had their moments in the first half but striker Mikael Ishak wasted two fine chances while Yegbe found the side-netting.

Richards timed to perfection a tackle on Allahyar Sayyadmanesh as the Iranian winger raced towards goal, but Palace continued to dominate early in the second half with Strand Larsen and the busy Quinten Timber threatening.
