A presidential ordinance of 13 September 2026 created the preliminary organising committee for the Democratic Republic of Congo’s national dialogue. Its coordinator, deputy coordinator and members are all appointed by the head of state.

What the Ordinance Does

The ordinance of 13 September 2026 establishes a preliminary organising committee under the direct authority of the head of state. Its coordinator, deputy coordinator and members are all presidentially appointed.

An eleven-expert technical secretariat supports it, also designated by the presidency. The structure was contested publicly within a day of its publication.

What the Dialogue Is

The process is formally titled the national dialogue for peace, cohesion and the refounding of the state. President Felix Tshisekedi announced it on 27 August 2026.

It provides for consultations in all 26 provinces, followed by national assemblies in Kinshasa. The whole process is capped at three months.

Who Is Not Invited

Armed groups considered to be backed by foreign interests are excluded, including the AFC and M23. Tshisekedi has said the Doha process remains the appropriate framework for dealing with them.

That draws a firm line between a domestic political conversation and an armed conflict negotiation. Whether the two can be kept separate is the central question critics raise.

The Objection to the Structure

Emery Okundji of FONUS, part of the Coalition Article 64, has objected to the committee’s composition. Jean-Claude Katende, president of the rights organisation ASADHO, has said the country is going in a bad direction.

The Kabila-aligned movement Sauvons la RDC has also objected. The common argument is that a body appointed by one office cannot convene a national conversation.

What One Civil Society Group Is Asking For

The public expenditure observatory ODEP set out its position on 14 September 2026. It wants the AFC and M23 at the table without granting them political legitimacy.

It also refuses committee members drawn from the governing coalition and demands independent facilitators. It urges that the process be modelled on Congo’s sovereign national conference.

That conference is the country’s reference point for an inclusive constitutional process. It was held in the early 1990s.

Where the Church Sits

On 16 September the Catholic bishops’ conference, through its justice and peace commission, hosted a panel on the conditions for the dialogue. Government spokesman Patrick Muyaya sat alongside the opposition figure Martin Fayulu and the former minister Marie-Ange Mushobekwa.

Convening government and opposition at one table is the church’s traditional role in Congolese politics. The panel discussed conditions rather than endorsing or rejecting the process.

A Claim We Are Not Repeating

A statement attributed to the bishops’ conference criticising the dialogue has circulated widely. Fact-checkers have established that the video dates from June 2026 and concerns a proposed constitutional change rather than the dialogue.

We are flagging it because it has shaped much of the coverage. The bishops’ conference has not issued the criticism being attributed to it.

Why the Composition Question Is Not Procedural

A dialogue’s legitimacy rests on who convenes it as much as on who attends. Participants who believe the outcome is predetermined tend not to come.

That is the practical risk of an entirely presidential appointment. Empty chairs are what turns a national dialogue into a government consultation.

What It Means for People in Congo

For citizens in the 26 provinces, the consultations are the stage they would encounter. No schedule for them has been published.

For anyone in the east, the exclusion of the armed groups means this process does not address the conflict there. That remains with the Doha track.

What Is Not Yet Known

The committee’s members have not been listed publicly. No start date for the provincial consultations has been announced.

It is also unclear whether any of the objecting parties will take part. None has formally declined.

What to Watch

Whether opposition parties agree to participate. That is the test of whether the three-month process can begin at all.

Watch also for any revision of the committee’s composition. Adjusting it is the most obvious way to answer the objection.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the ordinance do?

It created the preliminary organising committee for Congo’s national dialogue on 13 September 2026.

Who appoints the committee?

The head of state appoints the coordinator, deputy coordinator and all members, as well as an eleven-expert technical secretariat.

How will the dialogue run?

Consultations in all 26 provinces, then national assemblies in Kinshasa, over a maximum of three months.

Who is excluded?

Armed groups considered backed by foreign interests, including the AFC and M23.

Where are those groups dealt with?

Through the Doha process, according to President Tshisekedi.

Has the Catholic bishops’ conference criticised the dialogue?

No. A widely shared statement attributed to it dates from June 2026 and concerns a proposed constitutional change.

Sources: Presidential ordinance of 13 September 2026 and Congolese press reporting, 14 to 17 September 2026; ODEP statement of 14 September 2026; Balobaki Check verification of the attributed bishops’ conference statement.

World.title: Benin and Rwanda Sign a Round of Cooperation Deals on Trade Worth About US$126,500 a Year
World.content:
RWANDA · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — What happened Benin’s president Romuald Wadagni met Paul Kagame in Kigali and signed cooperation instruments.

— What they cover Taxation, air transport, agriculture, digital technology, military cooperation, tourism and investment promotion.

— The trade behind it Two-way trade was about US$126,500 in 2024, counting both directions.

— What each sells Rwanda sent cranes, tractors and earthmoving equipment, and Benin sent secondhand clothing and wicker goods.

— The earlier framework A first set of agreements was signed in Cotonou in 2023, under Benin’s previous president.

— What the presidents asked for They directed their delegations to strengthen existing cooperation and identify new areas.

Seven areas of cooperation, two presidents, and a trading relationship worth less than a small apartment.

Kigali, where Benin’s president met Paul Kagame on 16 September (Photo: Emmanuelkwizera, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Benin’s president Romuald Wadagni met Rwanda’s president Paul Kagame in Kigali on 16 September 2026. The two countries signed cooperation instruments on the first day of a two-day official visit.

What Was Signed

The two governments signed cooperation instruments on the first day of a two-day visit. They cover taxation, air transport, agriculture, digital technology, military cooperation, tourism and investment promotion.

The presidents also directed their delegations to strengthen existing cooperation. They asked for work on the mobility of goods, services and skills.

The Number That Frames It

Two-way trade between Benin and Rwanda was about US$126,500 in 2024. That is the total in both directions for a full year.

Rwanda’s exports to Benin were about US$116,000 and Benin’s to Rwanda about US$10,500. These are not rounding errors in the figures; they are the figures.

What Each Country Actually Sells

Rwanda’s exports to Benin consist of cranes, tractors and earthmoving equipment. Benin’s exports to Rwanda are secondhand clothing and wicker goods.

Neither list suggests an established commercial relationship. They read as occasional shipments rather than trade flows.

The Growth Rates, in Context

Rwandan exports to Benin grew about 47.5 percent a year between 2019 and 2024. Beninese exports to Rwanda grew about 8.46 percent a year.

Growth rates on figures this small are not meaningful in the usual way. A single additional tractor moves the percentage.

Why Two Countries Sign Anyway

Cooperation instruments create the legal machinery that trade needs before it can exist. A double taxation agreement, an air services agreement and an investment protection framework are preconditions rather than results.

Neither country can trade with the other at scale without them. Signing them is what turning intention into possibility looks like.

The Distance Problem

Benin is on West Africa’s Atlantic coast and Rwanda is landlocked in East Africa. There is no direct road route and very limited direct air freight.

An air transport agreement is therefore among the more consequential items signed. Connectivity is the binding constraint on everything else.

What Came Before

A first set of agreements was signed in Cotonou in 2023, when Kagame visited Benin. Patrice Talon was Benin’s president at the time.

Wadagni took office this year. The current visit is described as moving from those accords toward concrete projects.

The Rest of the Visit

The first day also included a tribute at Rwanda’s genocide memorial. The two delegations took part in a five-kilometre walk.

Those elements are standard in Rwandan state visits. They signal the relationship’s tone rather than its substance.

What It Means for Business

For companies in either country, the useful question is whether an air freight route follows. Without one, the agreements remain paperwork.

For anyone watching African intra-continental trade, the case is instructive. Two willing governments and almost no trade is the normal starting point rather than the exception.

What Is Not Yet Known

Neither government published the full text or a complete list of the instruments signed. No investment figure or project was announced.

It is also unclear when the agreements take effect. Ratification timelines have not been given.

What to Watch

Whether a direct air link or freight arrangement follows. That is the single change that would make the rest usable.

Watch also for the next trade figures. They are the only honest measure of whether any of this worked.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who met?

Benin’s president Romuald Wadagni and Rwanda’s president Paul Kagame, in Kigali on 16 September 2026.

What was signed?

Cooperation instruments covering taxation, air transport, agriculture, digital technology, military cooperation, tourism and investment promotion.

How much do the two countries trade?

About US$126,500 in 2024, counting both directions.

What do they sell each other?

Rwanda sends cranes, tractors and earthmoving equipment. Benin sends secondhand clothing and wicker goods.

Was there an earlier framework?

Yes. A first set of agreements was signed in Cotonou in 2023 under Benin’s previous president, Patrice Talon.

Were any investment figures announced?

No.

Sources: Ecofin Agency reporting on the Kigali meeting, 17 September 2026; bilateral trade data for 2024.

World.title: Guinea’s Media Regulator Issues a Formal Warning to France 24 Over One Word
World.content:
GUINEA · MEDIA

Key Facts — What happened Guinea’s media regulator issued a formal notice to France 24 on 16 September 2026.

— What it is not No sanction was imposed, and the broadcaster has not been taken off air.

— The wording at issue A broadcast described President Mamadi Doumbouya using a term meaning coup-installed president.

— What the regulator said It called the description inappropriate and degrading toward Guinea’s institutions.

— What the broadcaster did France 24 acknowledged the wording and said it would apologise and issue a correction.

— What could still happen The regulator has reserved the right to impose sanctions later.

A formal notice, not a ban, over an adjective the broadcaster has agreed to withdraw.

Conakry, where the media regulator issued its notice

Guinea’s media regulator has issued a formal notice to the French broadcaster France 24. The notice concerns a description of President Mamadi Doumbouya as a coup-installed president.

What Was Issued

Guinea’s High Authority for Communication issued a formal notice, known in French practice as a mise en demeure. It was dated 16 September 2026.

A formal notice is a warning that requires a response. It is not a suspension, and no immediate sanction was imposed.

Why This Distinction Matters

Several reports described France 24 as banned from broadcasting in Guinea. The regulator’s own statement says no immediate sanction was pronounced.

It does reserve the right to impose sanctions. That is a different position from having imposed one, and the difference is the story.

The Wording at Issue

A broadcast described President Mamadi Doumbouya with a term meaning coup-installed president. The regulator called the description inappropriate and degrading toward Guinea’s institutions.

The objection is to a single characterisation rather than to a report’s facts. That is what makes the case a press freedom question rather than an accuracy dispute.

How the Broadcaster Responded

France 24 acknowledged the use of the expression. It said it would present its apologies and issue a correction.

That response is what a formal notice is designed to produce. It also removes the most likely trigger for a sanction.

The Facts the Term Refers To

Doumbouya led a coup on 5 September 2021 that removed President Alpha Conde. He then headed a transitional government.

He won a presidential election on 28 December 2025 with 86.72 percent of the vote, on a turnout of 82.86 percent. The Supreme Court confirmed the result in early January 2026.

Why the Description Is Contested

Supporters point to the election and the court confirmation as the source of his current mandate. Critics point to how he first took power.

Both facts are on the record. A regulator ruling on which one may be used in a description is regulating characterisation rather than fact.

What a Formal Notice Can Lead To

Under most West African broadcasting frameworks, a formal notice is the first step in an escalating scale. Suspension and revocation sit further along it.

Whether the regulator proceeds usually depends on whether the broadcaster complies. France 24 has said it will.

What It Means for Viewers and Journalists

For viewers in Guinea, the channel remains available. Nothing announced changes access.

For journalists working in the country, the case marks where the regulator draws a line. It concerns how the head of state is described rather than what may be reported.

What Is Not Yet Known

The exact broadcast date is not settled. Reporting places it on 14 or 15 September 2026.

Nor is it known whether the regulator will consider the matter closed once the correction airs. It has not said what compliance would look like.

What to Watch

Whether the correction is broadcast and whether the regulator then closes the file. That would settle the case.

Watch also for similar notices to other foreign broadcasters. One notice is an incident and a pattern would be a policy.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has France 24 been banned in Guinea?

No. The regulator issued a formal notice and imposed no immediate sanction.

What was the objection?

A broadcast described President Mamadi Doumbouya using a term meaning coup-installed president.

How did France 24 respond?

It acknowledged the wording and said it would apologise and issue a correction.

When did Doumbouya take power?

He led a coup on 5 September 2021 that removed President Alpha Conde.

Was he elected?

Yes. He won the presidential election of 28 December 2025 with 86.72 percent of the vote.

Could a sanction still follow?

Yes. The regulator has reserved the right to impose sanctions.

Sources: Guinean High Authority for Communication notice of 16 September 2026, as reported by allAfrica, Tchadinfos and La Nouvelle Tribune.

World.title: Ghana’s Opposition Backs Some Constitutional Changes and Rejects the Process That Produced Them
World.content:
GHANA · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened Ghana’s opposition New Patriotic Party published its position on the review of the 1992 constitution.

— Who presented it Kojo Oppong Nkrumah, for the party’s policy coordination secretariat.

— What it supports Barring members of parliament from serving as ministers, a ceiling of 60 ministers, and electing local chief executives.

— What it rejects Expanding parliament from 276 to 300 seats, and a five-year presidential term.

— The bigger objection The party says the package amounts to a new constitution and demands a constituent assembly.

— The scale involved The review proposes amending 147 of 299 articles and adding 59 new provisions.

Yes to a minister cap and elected mayors, no to a bigger parliament, and no to the process itself.

Accra, where Ghana’s constitution review has become a party-political dispute (Photo: NASA Astronauts, Public domain via Wikimedia Commons)

Ghana’s opposition New Patriotic Party has set out its position on the review of the 1992 constitution. It supports several individual changes while rejecting the review process as partisan.

Who Is Speaking and From Where

The New Patriotic Party has been in opposition since losing the December 2024 election. John Mahama of the National Democratic Congress is president.

Kojo Oppong Nkrumah presented the position for the party’s policy coordination secretariat. The party notes that it rejected some of the same proposals when it was in government.

What the Party Supports

It backs barring members of parliament from serving as ministers, deputy ministers or regional ministers. It also supports a ceiling of 60 ministers.

It supports electing metropolitan, municipal and district chief executives rather than having them appointed. And it backs restricting members of parliament from sitting on public boards and procurement bodies.

What the Party Rejects

It opposes expanding parliament from 276 to 300 seats. It also opposes moving to a five-year presidential term.

Those two are the changes that would most directly affect the balance of power. That is the pattern in its position.

The Objection to the Whole Exercise

The party argues that the package amounts to the overhaul of a constitution and, in substance, the enactment of a new one. It points to 147 of 299 articles being amended and 59 new provisions added.

It says that in the absence of a constituent assembly, an attempt to bundle the government’s preferred amendments will not receive its support. That is a procedural objection rather than an argument about any single clause.

Why Separating Ministers From Parliament Matters

In Ghana’s system, members of parliament can serve as ministers. Critics say that gives the executive leverage over the legislature that is supposed to scrutinise it.

Barring the practice would change how much independent oversight parliament can offer. Both major parties have supported the idea in opposition more readily than in government.

Where the Review Came From

The Constitution Review Committee delivered its report to President Mahama on 22 December 2025. The review covers the 1992 constitution, which has governed Ghana since the return to multi-party rule.

A constituent or consultative assembly is the mechanism Ghana used to adopt that constitution. The opposition is asking for the same route this time.

The Money Question in the Background

Research by the Ghana Center for Democratic Development has documented the rising cost of seeking office. Campaign spending averaged about 389,803 cedis per parliamentary seat in 2016, a rise of 59 percent on 2012.

By 2020 it reported figures reaching as high as four million cedis. Its researcher Jacob Tetteh Ahuno has warned that this trend points toward state capture, where campaign financiers dictate what the state does.

The Party’s Own Timing

The New Patriotic Party holds its national officer elections on 19 September 2026. Positions taken publicly in the days before an internal election are read in that light.

Sulemana Tampuli Alhassan, the member of parliament for Gushegu, has been among those speaking on the proposals. He holds no national party office at present.

What It Means for Ghanaians

None of this changes any rule today. A constitutional amendment requires its own legislative process and, for entrenched provisions, a referendum.

The practical question is whether the two main parties can agree a process. Without that, a package of this size is unlikely to pass.

What Is Not Yet Known

The government has not responded to the demand for a constituent assembly. No timetable for putting amendments to parliament has been published.

It is also unclear which provisions the government regards as entrenched. Those are the ones that would require a referendum.

What to Watch

Whether the government engages with the constituent assembly demand. That is the procedural fork the whole exercise now turns on.

Watch also for the outcome of the opposition’s internal elections on 19 September. New party officers could revisit the position.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the New Patriotic Party in government?

No. It has been in opposition since losing the December 2024 election. John Mahama is president.

What does the party support?

Barring members of parliament from serving as ministers, a 60-minister ceiling, electing local chief executives, and restricting members from public boards.

What does it reject?

Expanding parliament from 276 to 300 seats and moving to a five-year presidential term.

What is its main objection?

That the package amounts to a new constitution and should go through a constituent assembly.

How large is the proposed change?

Amendments to 147 of 299 articles, plus 59 new provisions.

When was the review report delivered?

On 22 December 2025, to President Mahama.

Sources: New Patriotic Party position on the review of the 1992 constitution, 17 September 2026, as reported by MyJoyOnline; Constitution Review Committee report of December 2025; Ghana Center for Democratic Development research.

World.title: Guinea’s President Receives a Rusal Delegation Led by Russia’s Ambassador, With No Figures Announced
World.content:
GUINEA · MINING

Key Facts — What happened Guinea’s president received a Rusal delegation led by Russia’s ambassador at the presidential palace in Conakry.

— What was discussed Local processing of Guinean minerals, and Rusal’s existing bauxite and alumina operations.

— What Rusal asked for Presidential support for its investments in the country.

— What the president said He called local processing a strategic choice meant to last, and described it as essential and irreversible.

— What was not announced No investment figure, project or commitment was made public.

— The diplomatic note The ambassador conveyed greetings from President Vladimir Putin.

A presidential audience, greetings from Moscow, and not a single number on the table.

Bauxite mining, the business at the centre of the Conakry talks (Photo: Aboubacarkhoraa, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Guinea’s president Mamadi Doumbouya received a delegation from the Russian aluminium producer Rusal at the Palais Mohammed V in Conakry. The Russian ambassador to Guinea, Alexey Popov, led the delegation.

What Took Place

President Mamadi Doumbouya received the delegation at the Palais Mohammed V in Conakry. The Russian ambassador to Guinea, Alexey Popov, led it.

Popov conveyed greetings from President Vladimir Putin. Rusal asked for presidential support for its investments in Guinea.

What Was Actually Discussed

The subject was local transformation of Guinean minerals, meaning processing them in the country rather than exporting raw ore. Rusal’s existing presence is in bauxite and alumina.

Bauxite is the ore from which alumina is refined, and alumina is then smelted into aluminium. Guinea holds some of the world’s largest bauxite reserves.

What the President Said

Doumbouya described local processing as a strategic choice meant to last. He called the policy essential and irreversible.

That language is a signal to every foreign operator in the country, not only to Rusal. Guinea has been pushing miners toward domestic refining for several years.

What Was Not Said

No investment figure was announced. No project, site or timetable was made public by either side.

A presidential audience without numbers is a positioning exercise. We are reporting what was said rather than implying what might follow.

What Local Processing Actually Requires

An alumina refinery needs large, reliable electricity supply, water, port access and skilled operators. It is a far heavier commitment than a bauxite mine.

That is why exporting raw ore has remained the default. The policy pushes against the economics rather than with them.

What Is Already Being Built

Three alumina refineries are under construction in Guinea. A gold refinery is complete or close to it.

One of those projects is at Boffa, agreed in May 2026 with the Chinese producer Chalco. It is valued at about US$1.68 billion, which gives a sense of the capital such plants require.

The Programme This Sits Inside

Guinea has set out a long-term development programme running to 2040. It describes a fifteen-year effort valued at around US$200 billion, with a foundation phase of about US$65 billion to 2030.

Roughly seventy percent of that foundation phase is expected to come from private capital. The government has also set an ambition of reaching a B-plus sovereign credit rating.

The Iron Ore Project Nearby

Guinea’s Simandou iron ore project began operations in November 2025. Its first cargo of 200,000 tonnes reached China in January 2026.

It is no longer an undeveloped deposit, and it was not the subject of these talks. Rusal’s business in Guinea is bauxite and alumina.

What It Means for Guinea

For Guinean workers, refining creates more and better-paid jobs than mining alone. That is the case the government makes for the policy.

For the state, processed exports earn more per tonne. Whether that materialises depends on plants being built rather than announced.

What Is Not Yet Known

Neither party published a figure, a site or a timetable. It is unclear whether any Rusal commitment exists beyond the expression of interest.

The status of Guinea’s sovereign wealth fund has also not been updated publicly this year. Reports in late 2025 described it as created and as due to launch with about US$1 billion.

What to Watch

Any Rusal announcement naming a site or a sum. Without one, this meeting stands as diplomacy rather than investment.

Watch also for progress at the three refineries under construction. They are the measurable test of the local processing policy.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who met whom?

Guinea’s president Mamadi Doumbouya received a Rusal delegation led by Russia’s ambassador Alexey Popov in Conakry.

What was discussed?

Local processing of Guinean minerals and Rusal’s bauxite and alumina operations.

Was any investment announced?

No. No figure, project or timetable was made public.

What did the president say?

That local processing is a strategic choice meant to last, and is essential and irreversible.

What is being built already?

Three alumina refineries are under construction, including one at Boffa agreed with Chalco in May 2026.

Is Simandou part of this?

No. Simandou is an iron ore project that began operations in November 2025 and was not the subject of these talks.

Sources: Guinean presidency and press reporting on the Conakry meeting, 17 September 2026; Guinean government programme documents; Rio Tinto statements on Simandou operations.

World.title: Chad Says It Needs 8,000 Kilometres More Fibre, With Six Provinces Still Unconnected
World.content:
CHAD · TELECOMS

Key Facts — What happened Chad’s telecoms minister said the country needs about 8,000 kilometres more fibre for full coverage.

— Who he told Farouk Mollah Banna, the World Bank’s resident representative in Chad.

— What is missing Six provinces remain unconnected to the national backbone.

— How few people are online About 87 percent of Chadians were not using the internet as of 2024, according to the telecoms union.

— The single exit Chad’s only operational international connection runs through Cameroon.

— What broke the other one The eastern link became inoperative because of the conflict in Sudan.

Eight thousand kilometres short, six provinces dark, and one working way out of the country.

Fibre optic cable, the infrastructure Chad says it needs thousands more kilometres of (Photo: Profpcde, CC0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Chad needs about 8,000 kilometres of additional fibre optic cable to cover its territory. Telecoms and digital economy minister Haliki Choua Mahamat gave the figure on 15 September 2026.

What the Minister Said

Haliki Choua Mahamat, Chad’s minister for telecoms and the digital economy, put the shortfall at about 8,000 kilometres of fibre. He gave the figure to Farouk Mollah Banna, the World Bank’s resident representative.

He also said six provinces remain unconnected to the national backbone. Chad is a landlocked country of roughly 1.28 million square kilometres.

How the Existing Network Is Built

Chad’s backbone runs along three axes, to the west, the south and the east. The infrastructure is state-owned and operated by Sotel Tchad and Sudachad.

The eastern axis has become inoperative because of the conflict in Sudan. That leaves the connection through Cameroon as the country’s only working international exit.

Why a Single Exit Is a Problem

A landlocked country reaches the global internet through a neighbour’s cable. With one route, any fault or political disruption there cuts the whole country off.

The World Bank has recommended new links toward Libya and the Central African Republic. Both would add redundancy that Chad currently does not have.

How Few People Are Online

About 87 percent of Chadians were not using the internet as of 2024, according to the International Telecommunication Union. That is among the lowest usage rates anywhere.

Mobile phone penetration stands at about 44.3 percent, while mobile internet use is about 12.6 percent. People have phones and do not have data.

What Coverage Exists on Paper

Second-generation mobile coverage reaches about 86.9 percent of the population and third-generation about 84.5 percent. Fourth-generation coverage reaches about 60 percent.

Chad’s population is roughly 25 million. Coverage figures describe where a signal exists, not who can afford to use it.

The Money Already Committed

The World Bank approved a digital transformation project for Chad on 25 September 2024. It combines a grant of about US$92.2 million with about US$30 million of commercial financing.

The project runs to a closing date of 30 April 2029. That is an administrative deadline rather than a construction target.

An Earlier Programme and Its Financier

A separate state modernisation programme handed over its first phase at Sarh in December 2025. It is valued at about 175.1 million euros, roughly US$205 million, covering 1,200 kilometres of fibre and a national data centre.

Financing for that programme is linked to Exim Bank of China. The 1,200 kilometres it covers is planned capacity rather than cable already in the ground.

The Regional Link

Chad also has a segment of the trans-Saharan fibre route. Published lengths for it differ between about 503 and 550 kilometres depending on the source.

The wider project is valued at about 79 million euros, of which about 29 million comes from the European Union. It is one strand of a cross-Sahara connection rather than a national solution.

What It Means on the Ground

For businesses in the six unconnected provinces, the practical position is that fixed broadband is unavailable. Operations depend on mobile data or satellite links.

For anyone planning work in Chad, redundancy planning is not optional. A single international route means outages are a question of when.

What Is Not Yet Known

No construction timetable for the 8,000 kilometres has been published. Nor has a financing plan for that amount been set out.

The government has also not named the six unconnected provinces publicly. That detail would let businesses plan around the gap.

What to Watch

Any announcement of a second international route, toward Libya or the Central African Republic. That is the change that would most reduce Chad’s exposure.

Watch also for disbursement under the World Bank project. Approval in 2024 and construction are different things.

More: Africa news and analysis, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much fibre does Chad need?

About 8,000 kilometres more for full territorial coverage, according to its telecoms minister.

How many provinces are unconnected?

Six.

How many Chadians use the internet?

About 13 percent. Roughly 87 percent were not using it as of 2024.

How does Chad connect to the global internet?

Through a single operational route via Cameroon.

Why is the eastern route down?

It became inoperative because of the conflict in Sudan.

What funding exists?

A World Bank project of about US$122 million approved in September 2024, and a separate programme valued at about 175 million euros.

Sources: Statements by Chad’s telecoms and digital economy minister Haliki Choua Mahamat, 15 September 2026, as reported by Ecofin Agency; World Bank project documents; International Telecommunication Union data for 2024.

World.title: Ghana Hosts a Veteran Astronaut and Sets Out a Plan for Its Own Space Institution
World.content:
GHANA · SCIENCE

Key Facts — What happened Ghana’s foreign minister hosted the astronaut Koichi Wakata in Accra and set out national space plans.

— The plan Ghana is formulating a national space policy and intends to create its first dedicated space institution.

— The ambition stated Ablakwa spoke of Ghana producing the first African astronaut.

— Who the visitor is Wakata is a five-time space traveller who now leads Asia Pacific technology for the American firm Axiom Space.

— What Ghana has flown GhanaSat-1 was deployed from the International Space Station in 2017.

— What is not published No timetable, budget or legal framework for the new institution has been released.

A national space policy, a first institution, and an ambition named out loud in Accra.

A small satellite of the kind Ghanaian students built and had deployed in 2017 (Photo: NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio – Science and Technology Corporation/Kel Elkins, Public domain via Wikimedia Commons)
