That is why I made this association,” Zakharova said.

The Treaty of Georgievsk became the focus of political controversy in Georgia in August. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze described King Erekle II’s decision as “wise” and said there had been no alternative, arguing that it had saved Georgia as a state and nation. His remarks prompted a strong reaction from the opposition. His opponents accused him of portraying Russian imperial policy as historically beneficial to Georgia and of distorting the country’s history. The Georgiyevsky unit was established in Russia in early September. Its commander was named as Otar Romanov-Partskhaladze, Georgia’s former prosecutor-general. He lives in Russia, is under US and UK sanctions, and faces criminal charges in Georgia over allegations that he organised a contract killing. Russia describes him as a veteran of the war against Ukraine. The Georgian Orthodox Church strongly opposed the creation of a military unit named after Georgian Archimandrite Gabriel Urgebadze. The head of the Georgian Patriarchate’s press service said it was “particularly unacceptable that individual clergy of the Russian Orthodox Church support this initiative”.

According to Zakharova, Georgians have “long been helping” Russian-backed administrations operating in occupied territories of Ukraine and in Russian regions bordering Ukraine.

“Since the start of the special military operation, a large number of ethnic Georgians have voluntarily gone to the front and continue to take part, including in combat operations,” the Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman said.

Asked about the Georgian volunteers in the Russian army whom she had mentioned, Zakharova suggested “looking not at who is on which side, but at what values each side stands for”.

She cited Georgians fighting alongside people of other nationalities during World War Two as an example.

“At that time, 700,000 Georgians went to the front. And how many people did Georgia take in during the evacuation?” she said.

Zakharova also recalled Georgian soldier Meliton Kantaria, who, together with Russian soldier Mikhail Yegorov, raised the Soviet banner over the Reichstag in May 1945.

“Their feat became a symbol of the brotherhood in arms between Russians and Georgians,” Zakharova said.

“Our grandfathers and great-grandfathers were not fighting for one side or another. They were fighting Nazism, an ideology which held that the world should be divided along racial and national lines into those who deserved everything and those who deserved nothing except what those who deserved everything allowed them to have. That is what they fought against. And that is exactly what we are fighting against now,” she also noted.

Zakharova on family values and West seeking to ‘take them away’

“We and the Georgians are also allies in the fight to preserve the family,” Zakharova said, pointing to what she described as spiritual and moral values shared by the two peoples, including their way of life, traditions, art and culture.

She went on to say accuse Western countries of “trying to impose anti-values on Georgia”.

“We can see that a real struggle is taking place on this front as well. Together, we are protecting children from destructive ideology. They say that children are supposedly neither boys nor girls, that there is almost some kind of third gender. Or that they can be whatever they want: perhaps a chair, perhaps a saucepan. They can decide later in life. That is the kind of ideology they have there in the West,” the Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman said.

“Western countries are now trying to deprive Georgia of its historical memory and undermine the Orthodox foundations of society. This is exactly what we were talking about in the case of Armenia. They do not understand that this is impossible. Georgia has responded in a way that has further strengthened its commitment to respecting its own historical heritage,” Zakharova added.

Zakharova also spotlighted volunteers of the Georgiyevsky unit. She said she was certain what its members, whom she described as ethnic Georgians, were fighting for: “They are fighting for truth, for love of their history and their ancestors.”

“It is terrible to imagine what my grandfathers would have gone through if they had seen how [in Ukraine] the remains of the scoundrels Yevhen Konovalets and Andriy Melnyk [Ukrainian nationalists] were reburied. How they glorified the memory of Roman Shukhevych and Stepan Bandera. How they portrayed them as heroes and erected monuments to them.

How can we not fight against this? What will they turn us into afterwards? People like them, who have had their sexual organs changed 33 times? No, thank you,” she concluded.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s OTS strategy: unified approach spanning security to energy corridors and from national values to international prestige
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 17. The objectives facing the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) are no longer limited solely to preserving cultural and humanitarian ties. The organization is evolving into a vital platform where political, economic, energy, transport, and security interests across a vast geography are harmonized; Azerbaijan’s role in this process is clearly evident in the approaches outlined by President Ilham Aliyev in his recent address. Baku’s simultaneous hosting of religious leaders and heads of security agencies from OTS countries demonstrates Azerbaijan’s standing within the organization as a reliable platform, an initiator, and an active partner.

Baku becomes key venue for dialogue within OTS

Recent events in Baku are of particular significance in assessing Azerbaijan’s role within the OTS. Just days ago, religious leaders representing the organization's member states were received by President Ilham Aliyev, followed by a gathering in Baku of the heads of security councils from OTS member states for the council's fifth meeting. The fact that these events took place in the same location within a short timeframe should be viewed not merely as a coincidence of the diplomatic calendar, but as an indication of the systematic and multifaceted relationship established between Azerbaijan and the OTS. It's not merely a matter of hosting events here. The agenda of discussions within the framework of the OTS covers a broad spectrum, ranging from international relations and security to multiculturalism, trade, transport, and humanitarian cooperation. In this regard, Baku’s emergence as a reliable venue for discussing diverse issues highlights the multifaceted nature of Azerbaijan’s position within the organization.

The current stature of the OTS is the logical outcome of its development history. The organization was founded at the historic Summit held in Nakhchivan in 2009. At that summit, Azerbaijan, Türkiye, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan signed the Nakhchivan Agreement on the Establishment of the Cooperation Council of Turkic-Speaking States. The agreement entered into force in November 2010, and the organization's institutional framework was subsequently expanded. According to the OTS itself, the informal Summit held in Shusha in 2024 also marked a significant milestone in the organization's development.

Today, the primary strategic goal is to transform the OTS into a leading international organization. To achieve this, alongside the political will of the member states, there exists significant potential in terms of their economic, geographic, energy, transport, and human resources. President Ilham Aliyev’s address highlighted the strategic aim of more effectively harnessing this potential and consolidating it into a unified force.

New format originating in Shusha: annual meeting not enough

One of Azerbaijan’s initiatives for the development of the OTS is the holding of informal summits for heads of state. Although traditional summits are held regularly, the organization determined that, given the rapidly changing international landscape, a single annual gathering of heads of state was insufficient. Consequently, a proposal was made to establish an additional informal meeting format—an initiative that was realized with the support of partner nations. The inaugural meeting of this kind took place in Shusha, and the format has since continued in other countries.

The choice of Shusha holds particular political and symbolic significance. The 2024 Shusha Summit served as a platform for discussions on the OTS agenda regarding transport, connectivity, and climate action, resulting in the adoption of key documents, including the Karabakh Declaration. An official statement from the OTS describes the meeting held in Shusha as a significant milestone in strengthening the organization's cooperation and the unity of the Turkic world.

Thus, Azerbaijan's initiative goes beyond merely establishing a new meeting format. The primary objective is to foster a political dialogue within the OTS that is more dynamic, responsive, and sustained.

Energy and transport security enhance the geopolitical weight of the OTS

The vast geographical expanse spanned by the OTS member states grants the organization a significant advantage. Energy and transport routes of vital importance—not only to the member states but also to the broader region—traverse this territory. Consequently, assessing the role of the OTS solely within the context of political and humanitarian cooperation fails to fully reflect the organization's true potential.

President Ilham Aliyev’s approach presents energy security and transport connectivity as integral components of overall security because long-term regional stability and economic development are difficult to achieve without the reliable supply of energy resources and the connectivity required for the secure transportation of goods. This is also linked to the growing interest—in both the western and eastern parts of the OTS space—in the organization's role regarding connectivity, transport, energy security, and general security.

Natural resources are also a significant factor in this context. OTS countries possess vast natural resources, and these resources play a role in ensuring the economic resilience of states, the well-being of peoples, and, in a broader sense, the stability of the global economy. The importance of energy security is further heightened, particularly at a time when complex geopolitical situations exist along state borders.

Azerbaijan holds a special place in this system due to its geographical location. On one hand, the country acts as a supplier of energy resources to global markets; on the other, it utilizes its transit capabilities to transport energy resources originating from Central Asian countries—via the Caspian Sea—to international markets. Its location at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, combined with close ties to Türkiye and the Central Asian member states of the OTS, further enhances the role Azerbaijan plays in energy and transport security projects.

In this context, transport and energy projects are not merely economic endeavors for Azerbaijan; they also serve as instruments for strengthening strategic connectivity across the OTS region.

Bilateral relations form the backbone of multilateral cooperation within the OTS

Another crucial aspect of strengthening the OTS is the deepening of bilateral relations among member states. Azerbaijan pursues an active policy in this area as well. The numerous visits by President Ilham Aliyev to OTS countries, as well as visits by the leaders of those states to Azerbaijan, demonstrate the intensity of the mutual political dialogue.

Azerbaijan has signed treaties and declarations on alliance with Türkiye, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. These documents reflect the high political level of bilateral relations and lay the groundwork for developing cooperation in specific areas.

Parallel processes are also underway in the economic sphere. Azerbaijan has established joint investment funds with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Kyrgyzstan, and work continues on attracting and mobilizing mutual investments. These mechanisms enable political relations to be complemented by economic substance.

This approach is underpinned by one of Azerbaijan's foreign policy priorities. As President Ilham Aliyev has stated, the Turkic world represents a family space for Azerbaijan, and developing relations with this region is a key direction of its foreign policy. Consequently, cooperation with the OTS is not an isolated or sporadic element of Azerbaijan's foreign policy, but rather an integral part of a broader strategic course.

Shared ethnic roots complement political and economic cooperation

One of the features distinguishing the OTS from other international organizations is the existence of shared ethnic, historical, cultural, and linguistic ties among its members. Given that such organizations are not widespread in the international system, the spiritual foundation possessed by the OTS represents a significant advantage.

While political and economic interests may form the basis of interstate relations, the historical and cultural affinity existing between peoples renders these relations more enduring. Shared linguistic elements, cultural similarities, common ethnic roots, and spiritual closeness create additional opportunities for strengthening solidarity within the OTS. These factors enable the organization to evolve not merely into a mechanism for intergovernmental cooperation, but also into a platform for fostering connections between peoples.

This unity can also serve as one of the ideological pillars for the future development of the OTS. However, the key lies in approaching the preservation of national identity and spiritual values ​​not as a means of confrontation with other nations, but as a way to reinforce the member states' commitment to their own historical and cultural heritage.

Stability ranks among the economic advantages of OTS space

In today's international system, stability and security are not merely political issues; they are also fundamental prerequisites for economic development. It is difficult to attract a steady flow of investment, technology, and innovation to a country lacking political and economic stability. In this regard, maintaining stability within the OTS region is a key factor that enhances the organization's development potential.

As noted in President Ilham Aliyev's address, the growth of industrial production, positive economic indicators, and the stability of financial systems within the OTS region stand out against a global backdrop of economic stagnation, decline, and various socio-economic challenges. This dynamic is significant for strengthening the economic capabilities of the member states.

At the meeting held in Baku, OTS Secretary General Kubanychbek Omuraliev also presented data regarding the economic potential of the organization's region. According to him, the aggregate GDP of the OTS region stands at $2.4 trillion, a figure that places it roughly 12th globally. Meanwhile, the organization's trade turnover amounts to $1.7 trillion. These figures demonstrate that the OTS is not merely a political and cultural union, but also a region with immense economic potential.

The combination of economic opportunities with political stability, energy resources, and transport connections creates additional grounds for enhancing the role of the OTS in the international system.

Youth issues represent a long-term dimension of security

One of the key factors shaping the future of the OTS is the set of values ​​that mold the younger generation. The relatively young populations of the member states and the observed demographic growth constitute a significant advantage for the organization. At a time when concerns regarding rapid population decline are mounting in a number of countries, the opposite trend observed within the OTS region fosters significant human capital for the future.

However, a demographic advantage does not automatically translate into an economic one. Population growth must be accompanied by active economic policies, the expansion of social infrastructure, and the creation of new jobs. Otherwise, rapid growth could lead to certain economic and social challenges. President Ilham Aliyev’s speech highlighted the positive dynamics observed in addressing issues related to economic growth and social welfare across OTS countries.

Another aspect of the youth issue concerns national self-awareness and moral values. A shared characteristic of OTS countries is their commitment to their national and moral principles. In this regard, raising the younger generation in a spirit of patriotism and commitment to national principles and moral values ​​is not merely a matter of upbringing; it is a strategic priority linked to the long-term stability of states.

The foundation of Azerbaijan's youth policy was established within the framework of the state policy initiated by the National Leader Heydar Aliyev. Key aspects of this policy include paying attention to and caring for young people, creating conditions for their development, strengthening their role and standing in society, and fostering a spirit of patriotism.

This approach can also be advanced at the level of the OTS. It is essential to involve young people in processes not merely as subjects of decisions made about them, but as active participants whose views and positions are heard. Gathering their input, bringing together youth from various countries, and expanding their mutual interactions can strengthen the organization's future social foundation.

Concept of security no longer limited to military threats alone

The expansion of the OTS security agenda holds a special place in Azerbaijan's own agenda. The continuation of wars in surrounding regions, the expansion of their geographical scope, and the increasingly overt nature of the conflicts bring the issue of regional security to the forefront. This reality is of particular significance for Azerbaijan; the presence of states engaged in warfare to both the country's north and south heightens the sensitivity of the security environment.

In such a situation, the need to strengthen coordination among the security structures of the OTS countries becomes apparent. Information exchange, particularly the sharing of operational intelligence, joint action, coordination against existing threats, and the proactive identification and prevention of potential risks must become core elements of the security system.

In this context, the agenda of the fifth meeting of Security Councils held in Baku is no coincidence, either. The gathering of security agencies facilitates not only the discussion of current challenges but also the comparison of experiences across different nations, the identification of vulnerabilities, and the refinement of mechanisms to prevent threats. According to information released by the Secretary General of the OTS, the recent holding of several high-level meetings across the organization's region—covering security and other areas—demonstrates the expansion of this agenda. Meetings of interior ministers in Astana (Kazakhstan) and prosecutors general in Turkistan have taken place; religious leaders were received by President Ilham Aliyev two days prior to the meeting in Baku; and a meeting of defense industry chiefs is scheduled for October 1. It was also noted that 63 mechanisms and platforms, ranging from foreign policy to culture, operate within the framework of the OTS.

These figures and events indicate that OTS cooperation is no longer limited to meetings between heads of state; rather, multi-level mechanisms for interaction among various government agencies have been established.

Ideological threats create new security agenda

In the modern era, threats to state security are not limited to border violations or physical attacks. Ideological influences exerted through the information space, media, social platforms, and various communication channels can also impact the internal stability of states.

President Ilham Aliyev’s speech emphasizes the importance of a joint struggle against these threats. The focus here is on preventing ideological provocations that run counter to the interests of countries and peoples. Particular attention is drawn to influence exerted through media outlets reportedly funded by centers located far beyond national borders. According to the approach presented by President Ilham Aliyev, such financing could serve the aims of undermining the state structure, disrupting social solidarity, and instilling narratives and values ​​alien to society.

According to Azerbaijan’s position, efforts to counter such risks must be undertaken to safeguard national interests and the constitutional order. President Ilham Aliyev has stated that active measures are being taken in this regard in Azerbaijan and that significant results have been achieved.

It was also noted that "anti-national" networks operating within Azerbaijan—allegedly directed and funded from abroad—are rejected by the vast majority of society. A key point here is that adherence to national values, traditions, and ways of life stands as the prevailing trend in Azerbaijani society.

However, the fact that these threats are being countered does not mean they have been completely eliminated. On the contrary, given the potential for continued attempts to destabilize the situation, preventive mechanisms must be constantly strengthened.

Primary objective: to protect youth from informational and ideological threats

Youth is regarded as a particularly vulnerable group regarding the issue of ideological security. As noted in President Ilham Aliyev's speech, the younger generation—which is still in its formative stage and more susceptible to manipulation—is a primary target of external activities aimed at undermining state interests. Therefore, youth policy within the framework of the OTS (Organization of Turkic States) can be approached not merely as a matter of social and cultural cooperation, but as an issue of long-term security.

In this regard, it’s proposed to expand interaction among the youth organizations of OTS member states and to hold regular forums, conferences, and other events. The aim is to facilitate direct communication among young people from different countries, enhance their knowledge of shared history and culture, and ensure that the bonds between kindred nations are preserved within the new generation.

Such an approach serves as more than just a means to counter ideological influences; it is also a long-term mechanism for shaping the human capital that will underpin the OTS's future political, economic, and social ties. Fostering closer mutual understanding among young people can create a social foundation for future cooperation in business, science, education, technology, culture, and other fields.

New phase for OTS: transforming existing potential into tangible strength

The task facing the OTS countries is not merely to enumerate existing opportunities, but to translate them into concrete results through coordinated policy. Factors such as energy resources, transport corridors, a favorable geographic location, economic potential, a young population, a shared historical-cultural heritage, and political will can be viewed not as isolated advantages, but as elements of a unified strategic system.

Azerbaijan’s position in this process is particularly noteworthy. The country acts as both an energy producer and a transit state; it is situated at the crossroads of Europe and Asia; it actively cooperates with Central Asian nations and Türkiye; and it spearheads various political and institutional initiatives within the OTS.

The emphasis placed by the Kazakh side—during the meeting in Baku—on the development of Trans-Caspian infrastructure and the significance of the Middle Corridor underscores the practical importance of this direction. Aida Balayeva, Deputy Chair of the Security Council of Kazakhstan, highlighted the importance of economic cooperation with Azerbaijan, Trans-Caspian infrastructure, and the project to establish a fiber-optic communication link across the bed of the Caspian Sea. President Ilham Aliyev noted that the fiber-optic cable project is nearing completion and holds significant importance for Azerbaijan-Kazakhstan relations as well as for the broader region, including the OTS space.

These facts demonstrate that cooperation within the OTS is not limited to political declarations but is also reinforced by tangible infrastructure projects.

Experience of independence shapes shared political memory

For a significant number of OTS countries, the restoration of independence represents a relatively recent stage in their modern statehood history. As President Ilham Aliyev pointed out, setting aside their ancient statehood legacies, the modern statehood of most member countries spans approximately 35 years. Azerbaijan restored its state independence in 1991; Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan also regained their independence during the same period.

Each of these countries faced unique challenges on its post-independence path of development. Azerbaijan, too, has navigated complex trials. However, as emphasized in the President's speech, this phase has been both challenging and honorable; having emerged from the most complex trials, the countries now find themselves in a position where they have left behind a significant portion of the global problems they once faced.

This experience forms another foundation for political solidarity within the OTS. The importance of the history of statehood, independence, and the preservation of national sovereignty constitutes a crucial element of the shared political memory for the organization's member states.

Azerbaijan’s approach: security and development inseparable

The overarching logic of President Ilham Aliyev’s address regarding the OTS highlights two complementary directions: security and development. Without security, it is impossible to create a sustainable environment for economic development, investment, technology, and innovation. At the same time, the expansion of economic opportunities and the strengthening of transport and energy connections are factors that reinforce the stability of states and societies.

For this reason, the approach Azerbaijan advocates within the framework of the OTS is based not only on a political and security agenda but also on economic and humanitarian components. Enhancing the organization’s international standing, strengthening energy and transport corridors, deepening bilateral relations, increasing mutual investments, expanding ties among youth, and strengthening coordination against ideological threats are all facets of the same strategic picture.

Baku’s recent hosting of religious leaders and high-ranking security officials from the OTS serves as a practical manifestation of this approach. The organization’s agenda is steadily expanding, with mechanisms across various fields complementing one another. As noted by the Secretary General of the OTS, there are currently 63 mechanisms and platforms—ranging from foreign policy to culture—where not only are meetings held, but concrete decisions are adopted and tasks set by the leaders are implemented.

Primary task ahead: transforming potential into a leading international force

The OTS now faces a more complex stage of development. The organization’s potential—encompassing political, economic, geographic, energy, transport, and human capital assets—creates a solid foundation for it to play a greater role in the international system. However, transforming this potential into tangible power requires coordination, mutual trust, and sustained cooperation on concrete projects among member states.

In this process, Azerbaijan positions itself not merely as one of the member states, but as a country that advances initiatives, organizes dialogue across various formats, and serves as a key link connecting the OTS region through its energy and transport capabilities.

In this regard, Azerbaijan’s stance is clear: developing ties with the Turkic world is a top foreign policy priority, and the OTS serves as the multilateral institutional platform for this policy. Strengthening the organization is viewed as a course of action that aligns not only with Azerbaijan’s national interests but also with the shared interests of all member states. Ultimately, the future of the OTS will depend not only on the shared history and cultural affinity of its members but also on the extent to which this affinity translates into modern statehood, economic cooperation, energy security, transport connectivity, and collective security mechanisms. The approach put forward by Azerbaijan is aimed precisely at facilitating this transition.

The central theme of President Ilham Aliyev’s address is that the OTS countries possess shared interests across a vast geography, significant economic and energy potential, vital transport capabilities, a young population, historical-cultural ties, and the political will to cooperate. Coordinating these resources could further strengthen the organization's international standing.

The objective ahead is clearly defined: to transform the Organization of Turkic States into a leading international institution through joint efforts. Azerbaijan’s role in this process is grounded in taking the initiative, acting as a reliable partner, and providing a platform for regional and international cooperation. The successive meetings in Baku, the informal summit format launched in Shusha, energy and transport projects, bilateral alliance relations, investment funds, and growing coordination in the security sphere demonstrate that a broad institutional and practical foundation for this objective has already been established.

World.title: Melbourne woman set to be extradited after gun allegedly linked to Sydney killing
World.content:
Police are seeking to extradite a woman from Melbourne after detectives allege they have linked a gun from two Sydney shootings to the mistaken identity gangland murder of Marco Tapia.

Mr Tapia, 23, died after masked gunmen stormed his Glen Alpine home and shot him dead on September 1.

The university student was the sixth mistaken identity murder linked to Sydney's underworld war in the space of 18 months.

Police at the scene of the Glen Alpine home over a fortnight ago. (ABC News)

In documents obtained by the ABC from a Victorian court, NSW Police will allege a group of Melbourne men were involved in two shootings linked to the ongoing feud between the Alameddine crime family and the self-proclaimed "Coconut Cartel".

"The history of that conflict is characterised by retaliatory violence, firearm offences and acts of intimidation," police allege in a document submitted to a Magistrates Court this week.

The Coconut Cartel, which takes its name from a historic slur against Pasifika people, and the Alameddines are playing out a violent underworld war on Sydney's streets while their leaders remain offshore.

Police have stated that Mr Tapia was not involved in organised crime and that detectives believe his death was tragically an error by his killers.

Superintendent Joe Doueihi yesterday alleged the teenagers arrested were "clumsy" in their actions. (ABC News)

Two teenagers on Thursday were charged over their alleged roles in the murder of Mr Tapia.

The Melbourne woman, 26-year-old Amenah Abusud, is alleged to have been "recruited by an organised crime network, was tasked, and received payments to participate" in two shootings prior to Mr Tapia's death.

The ABC understands the NSW Police Raptor Squad are also attempting to extradite three other Melbourne men over their alleged involvement in the two shootings.

Police, in the court documents, allege the weapon used in the two shootings was also used to kill Mr Tapia.

According to the court documents the woman and several men set off from Donnybrook, in Melbourne's north, in a Hyundai two days before the shooting of Mr Tapia.

Police allege Ms Abusud "utilises" the same Hyundai.

Court documents state police tracked the vehicle at Campbelltown before CCTV captured the group of men at a local AirBnB.

Boosted powers to target Sydney's gangsters, but police face a new problem They are the extraordinary powers the premier has promised to expand in a bid to combat gangland violence, but they face a major test in this era of organised crime.

A day before Mr Tapia's shooting, documents allege, the group broke into and shot up a home in Hurstville before its owner received a threatening message from an international number on WhatsApp.

Hours later the document states the same group shot up parked cars at a home in Turrella.

Police said in their statement of alleged facts that blood from one of the shootings identified one of the Melbourne men and gun cartridges were matched to a third shooting: the death of Mr Tapia a day later at Glen Alpine.

Investigators from the NSW Police's Raptor Squad are seeking to have Ms Abusud extradited from Victoria today, alleging she "is at risk of attempting to flee the country".

Police are seeking the woman's transfer interstate over charges related to the shootings at Turrella and Hurstville, but not in relation to the shooting of Mr Tapia.

World.title: How the WA government tried — and failed — to limit payouts to abuse survivors
World.content:
The Western Australian government was trying to have its cake and eat it too when it walked into the Court of Appeal last week.

Child sexual abuse survivor Dion Barber was last year awarded nearly $3 million in compensation for abuse he suffered while in state care in the 1980s and 1990s.

The government wanted to argue it was too much, or shouldn’t have been given at all — a case even the most talented politician wouldn't be able to sell to the public.

Man awarded almost $3 million for sexual abuse in state care Perth man Dion Barber, who was repeatedly sexually abused at successive state care placements, is awarded almost $3 million in compensation by a judge.

So it tried to have it both ways.

It paid Mr Barber's compensation in full and promised it wouldn't take anything back if it was successful in its appeal.

But at the same time, the government argued the court had made errors in its decision, including that it should be "immune from liability" because staff acted in good faith.

That's significant because, as the government told the court, there are almost 200 people with similar circumstances currently seeking compensation from the state.

A successful appeal would have effectively created a double standard — one for Mr Barber, and one for everyone who came after him.

Setting a precedent

The three Supreme Court justices who heard the government's case — including Chief Justice Peter Quinlan — rejected it on the same day, and this week published their reasons for doing so.

The judges dismissed the case, saying it was "not an appropriate exercise" of the Supreme Court's judicial powers. (ABC News: Jack Stevenson)

In their view, the state government was seeking a decision "to facilitate its negotiation on those many other claims, presumably on a basis more favourable than the outcome in Mr Barber's case".

What the appeal against Dion Barber's win could mean Less than a decade after the door opened for victims of historic child sexual abuse to seek justice in WA, abuse survivors could be at risk of having that door closed again, writes Cason Ho.

"It would be inappropriate," the judges wrote, for the court to trawl back through the "deeply personal" evidence of the case "solely for the purpose of facilitating the state's resolution of other claims".

"If the state wishes to deny another claim, it ought to do so, openly and transparently, in the ordinary course of litigation … rather than on the basis of an advisory opinion from this court."

In other words, if the government wants to reduce compensation for a victim-survivor, it needs to say it to their face, and the face of every Western Australian.

A question of liability

Questioned about the decision on Tuesday, WA Premier Roger Cook said the government acted on "the best legal advice".

"We were seeking to clarify elements of the law so that we could provide justice to more people faster," he said.

Roger Cook says the government has been seeking a reference point for similar cases. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Having a clear reference point on damages, and clear answers on how the courts interpret the law, can narrow the scope of negotiations with those remaining 200 people.

But what the premier didn't mention — and what the Court of Appeal highlighted — was that a reference point could also help reduce the amount the state had to pay, or if they would have to pay at all.

"If the Christian Brothers went to the Court of Appeal to say that we knowingly sent a child into the hands of a paedophile but we don't want to be found liable or responsible for it, there would be outrage in the parliament, outrage by the government and outrage in the community," Mr Barber's lawyer, Hugo Seymour, told 102.5 ABC Perth last week.

Dion Barber's lawyer, Hugo Seymour (left), says the government is to blame. (ABC News: David Weber)

"Yet that's exactly what the Department of Communities and the Insurance Commission of WA have done in the name of the state."

Shouting match

The Insurance Commission is the state government's insurer. A spokesperson declined to answer questions, only saying: "We respect the decision of the Court of Appeal."

Shadow Attorney-General Nick Goiran said questions about the commission's conduct went beyond Mr Barber's case.

Nick Goiran wants the government insurer to change its approach. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"When it comes to the culture of handling these claims, these very difficult, sensitive claims for victims of sexual abuse, the organisation that needs to change is the Insurance Commission," he said.

"And that's where [Treasuer] Rita Saffioti needs to step up and do something about it."

Saffioti was asked about the matter during question time and pointed to laws Labor passed which removed a time limit restricting when survivors could bring legal action.

WA Deputy Premier Saffioti engaged in a parliament shouting match over the matter. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"Over $110 million has been paid to over 300 victims in this state," she told parliament, before getting into a shouting match with the opposition.

"The attorney-general and I always look at how we can make sure we get the best outcome for Western Australians."

'Further torment'

Behind all of those arguments though is Mr Barber, who despite the government's assurances, said the last year had been "further torment".

Dion Barber is still waiting for an apology from the government. (ABC News: David Weber)

Mr Barber has also yet to receive an apology from the government.

"It would be nice to get in one sense, but they're just words," he told 102.5 ABC Perth.

" If they're not really meant, then I'd rather see change. Change would be a better apology. "

How the government chooses to resolve those 200 remaining cases will give an indication of whether this final resolution of Mr Barber's case has prompted the change he hopes for.

World.title: Qld 18yo charged with violent extremist offences after FBI tip-off
World.content:
An 18-year-old Queenslander has been charged with extremist offences after allegedly running social media channels supporting violence against Muslims, Jews and migrants.

Police said the investigation was sparked by a report from the FBI alleging an Australian user was spreading extremist content on a social media platform.

Officers from the Queensland Joint Counter Terrorism Team executed a search warrant at a home in Warner, north of Brisbane, on May 27, seizing several electronic devices.

It is alleged the man was operating multiple social media channels supporting violence against people of Muslim, Jewish, and migrant backgrounds.

Police said forensic examination of the devices allegedly revealed extremist content and child abuse material.

The man has been charged with 30 offences including using a carriage service to transmit violent extremist material, using a carriage service to harass or cause offence, and possessing or controlling child abuse material.

He first appeared in court on May 27 and was remanded in custody.

He is expected to reappear in Pine River Magistrates Court today.

World.title: First Nations netballers driving change, bringing cultural safety
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

While netball may be Australian girls' and women's top participation team sport, it has long fallen short of producing — or at least nurturing — elite Indigenous talent.

Just three Indigenous Australian women have represented the Diamonds: Marcia Ella-Duncan, Sharon Finnan-White and, after a 22-year gap, Donnell Wallam.

In 2024, Wallam left Australia for New Zealand, taking a swipe at her former club, the Firebirds, on the way out.

At the time, she wrote that the New Zealand clubs' "respect for inclusion and culture" was a key factor in her decision to leave, while she eventually returned to the Sunshine Coast Lightning this year.

Netball Australia was not idly watching.

As accusations of a 'toxic culture' at the Firebirds were aired, the governing body launched an investigation and kickstarted a series of measures to enshrine 'cultural safety' for First Nations athletes in the sport.

This included the introduction of Australia's inaugural First Nations team, the Black Swans, following the appointment of Ali Tucker-Munro, Netball Australia's General Manager First Nations and former Diamonds squad member.

This is the third year the First Nations Tournament has run. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Tucker-Munro was also influential in establishing the First Nations Tournament, a yearly national championship currently being held in Melbourne, and the Spirit Series, which launched in 2026 and saw the Black Swans go undefeated against Australia's Pacific neighbours.

Speaking from the State Netball and Hockey Centre, Tucker-Munro, alongside players Gabby Coffey and Scarlet Jauncey, said the measures had begun to address the lack of visible role models for First Nations netballers, with more work to be done.

Embraced in Alice Springs

Twenty-six-year-old Coffey, representing the Northern Territory, is one of several First Nations netballers who have been stuck at the cusp of national competition.

Gabby Coffey says it means a lot to bring Indigenous netballers together for the tournament. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

The defender spent four years as a Melbourne Vixens training partner before eventually making the decision to move to the UK to further her netball career.

She represented Birmingham over two seasons, and has since returned to Alice Springs.

Coffey had seen the writing on the wall at the Vixens.

"I knew there wasn't much movement in their defensive end, and the same with a lot of defensive ends around Australia," Coffey told ABC Sport.

While she has not given up on a professional career, she is also at peace with the idea that her role may be to support other First Nations athletes with their sporting aspirations.

The Wiradjuri woman grew up in Alice Springs, away from mob and country, but remembers being embraced by the community in Arrente.

Coffey (left) played for Birmingham in England's top competition. (Getty Images: Morgan Harlow)

"When you grow up on other Indigenous land and tell people you're Indigenous, they pull you into their culture, so [my family and I] were super lucky and blessed to grow up in the centre of Australia where arguably their Indigenous culture is very sacred and traditional," she said.

Determined to pursue netball, she was advised by coach Gillian Lee to move down south, and remembers the transition to Melbourne as a difficult one.

"It was really hard being away from home," Coffey said.

"I was really lucky with the team I entered [the Vixens] and the support I did have, but it's not the same for everyone. There's a lot of girls who do get those opportunities to move and then don't last because there's just not that support in place."

Hailing from the Northern Territory, Coffey said, was an additional barrier.

"Even with competitions like these, we don't get together until we're here, and we're training away from each other, so it can be quite a challenge."

Visible Indigenous role models key

Asked what more could be done to help First Nations netballers make it to the elite level, Coffey said role models were key.

"If you can't see it, you can't be it," she said, pointing out that there are only two Indigenous players currently in Super Netball.

Coffey says it is important to have visible role models. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Coffey said her own experience of spending multiple years as a train-on player, without breaking into the elite environment, showed how difficult it was to make it into a professional team in Australia.

"We get a number of internationals [coming to Super Netball], which I think makes the game better and more exciting, and I don't think [that] should be restricted," she said.

"But I do think there should be more focus on bringing Indigenous girls into the elite level."

She pointed to Netball Australia's plans to introduce two new teams into the competition, saying this would open further list spots.

A New Zealand team, she added, may take pressure away from the Australian players vying for contracts.

Scarlet Jauncey has spent the last year as a training partner for the West Coast Fever, pinching herself to line up on names like Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard at training.

Scarlet Jauncey is representing Western Australia, and has captained the Black Swans. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

A Yaruwu woman from Rubibi/Broome in Western Australia, Jauncey agreed with Coffey that cutting international talent was not a solution.

"We're happy to be playing against the best in the world, that's what we want," the defender said.

Like many of her teammates, Jauncey grew up idolising Wallam.

"I think it just gives us something to strive towards, knowing that we can be in that space," she said.

In 2025, Jauncey captained the Black Swans, in turn becoming a role model to other First Nations players.

"It was the best tournament I've played in, the best teams I've been with," she said.

"I think just being able to come to First Nations tournaments and having that connection with each other has been really great."

Jauncey in action during this year's tournament. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Coffey agreed, saying the experience had given her "goosebumps".

"I think it gives not only myself, but a lot of players so much power and push to keep going and play at the highest level," she said.

Cultural safety means listening to community

Tucker-Munro smiles when hearing the players' responses to playing for the Black Swans.

It has been one of her signature initiatives, alongside the First Nations Tournament and Spirit Series.

Ali Tucker-Munro is Netball Australia's general manager for First Nations. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

"These tournaments are aspirational in terms of trying to inspire the next generation of our kids — who we know love sport and netball in particular — to trial for their respective state and territory," she said.

"It's about the kids that are here this week wanting to aspire to take that next step into the big leagues in terms of Super Netball and Australian representation as well."

Tucker-Munro acknowledged that while it was important to bring First Nations netballers into elite environments, those environments had to be culturally safe.

"First Nations people come into these spaces with our culture and community on our back, as well as cheering us on, so you want to do them proud," she said.

"It's also a tough journey, especially for the kids who have to relocate, so it's about thinking strategically about how we can support them."

Players have enjoyed coming together in Melbourne for this year's tournament. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Since her appointment, the code has put in place a First Nations Cultural Council, and last year ran a cultural safety review in collaboration with community.

The review considered the perspectives of the wider netball workforce, including coaches and umpires as well as athletes

Tucker-Munro conceded there are "multi-faceted" barriers to having more elite Indigenous netballers, including financial constraints and geographical barriers to access.

"For too long our voice has been very silent," Tucker-Munro said.

"We're not a homogenous people, so it's really important that we make sure we're hearing the voices of many.

"One thing we're really big on in our community is not to do things for us or to us, you've got to do it with us.

"There's real intent and good will to actually drive some of this change across the sporting landscape of netball in Australia."

World.title: Shark attack rescuer struggling to forget the blood
World.content:
A man who responded to a shocking shark attack on Western Australia's Midwest coast says he is struggling to forget the sight of the blood.

Having surfed at Glenfield Beach in Geraldton for more than 20 years, Shannan Dunn had eagerly run up a steep sand dune to check the conditions on Monday morning.

He snapped a picture of the swell with another surfer, Mel Ismail, in the distance before running back to his car to put on his wetsuit.

Shannan Dunn took this photo of Mel Ismail minutes before the shark attack. (Supplied: Shannan Dunn)

Moments later, Mr Ismail was bitten by a shark.

"His board was about 5 metres away, and he had his arm up," Mr Dunn said.

" Then it only took a couple of seconds and I saw the blood all around him. "

Mr Dunn raced into the water and swam out in Mr Ismail's direction.

"I don't think I really hesitated; I just wanted to get to him as quick as I could," he said.

"He said, 'Shark — it's got my leg', and I decided I wasn't going to look at it."

DNA from the bitten board is being used to identify the shark species involved. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Assessing the damage

Mr Dunn said he "clumsily" paddled Mr Ismail to the beach, where a bystander made a makeshift tourniquet from a leg rope while another called Triple Zero (000).

"He had lost his foot from just above his ankle," Mr Dunn said.

"He … looked like he could fade out at any moment.

"We didn't know how much blood he had lost."

Shannan Dunn has been dreaming of the blood surrounding Mr Ismail. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Mr Dunn brought his four-wheel drive onto the beach and, along with some teenagers and the other bystanders, got Mr Ismail into the back to meet the paramedics.

"We just gunned it down the beach," he said.

The 56-year-old firefighter was rushed to the Geraldton Health Campus with serious injuries, where he remains in a stable condition.

A St John WA spokesperson said the first aid administered by those at the scene was "exceptional" and helped paramedics to rapidly transfer Mr Ismail to hospital.

"St John WA pays tribute to the quick thinking and skills of those on scene," they said.

"It was a credit to all who responded."

Mel Ismail remains in a stable condition and faces a long recovery. (Facebook)

Drawn to water

Mr Dunn returned to the scene of the frantic rescue on Thursday, three days on from the attack.

"When I look out to where the sets are and stuff, I can still envision the blood," he said.

" I'm still thinking about it at night as well, like, that's probably the worst part about it. "

Glenfield Beach reopened on Wednesday. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Despite the trauma, Mr Dunn plans to get back in the water sooner rather than later.

"I've given myself a week … if the conditions are right and there are enough people in the water, I'll probably give it a crack," he said.

"I don't think I'll be able to keep away from it for too long."

Glenfield Beach reopened on Wednesday morning, and the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD) confirmed it had stopped patrolling the area.

A DPIRD spokesperson said DNA from the damaged board and Mr Ismail's wetsuit was still being analysed to determine the species "most likely" behind the attack.

Long recovery ahead

Mr Dunn said Mr Ismail's family told him he was recovering well in hospital.

"It's looking very promising, I'd say, at this stage," Mr Dunn said.

"You've always got to touch a bit of wood, though."

Mr Dunn hoped he could reunite with Mr Ismail soon.

"Hopefully I don't bring back any bad memories from that day," Mr Dunn said.

"I'm hoping that he will be stoked to see us, as I'm just as stoked to see him, to be honest.

"I literally can't wait for that day, but it's only when he's ready."

World.title: Bushfire survivor builds fire-resistant tiny home kit that fits in ute tray
World.content:
Fiona Logge remembers struggling to stay calm while wading through the surf with her young family to escape the Black Summer bushfires.

In December 2019, their holiday home in Manyana on the New South Wales south coast had been cut off by the deadly Currowan State Forest bushfire.

Four months pregnant, Ms Logge said the family decided to evacuate when offered a spot in a passing boat packed with residents heading for a recovery centre in Ulladulla.

Firefighters at work on the Currowan fire between Batemans Bay and Ulladulla in 2019. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

She said the hardest moment came as she watched her husband and architect Adriano Pupilli swim back to shore, determined to save their home.

"Everyone was yelling from the boat, 'No, come back!'" Ms Logge said.

" It was pretty heart-wrenching. "

Returning days later, Mr Pupilli was stunned to discover the fire had come within metres of their property line but had left their home unscathed.

However, Ms Logge said the stress of the experience had left a heavy mental toll on the family.

Fiona Logge with her son, Max, and Adriano Pupilli. (ABC News: Monish Nand)

"I said to Adriano, 'We're going to do that again in five years' time.'"

Turning to architecture for a solution, Mr Pupilli created Casa Manyana — a bushfire-resistant modular home.

Nominated for two Australian architecture awards, Mr Pupilli said the project was an affordable housing option for bushfire-prone communities.

Flat-packed home for bushfire survivors

With a bathroom, loft bedroom and kitchenette, Casa Manyana comes with all the trappings of a modern tiny home.

It is also built to the second-highest bushfire attack level standard of BAL 40, meaning it can withstand high levels of ember attack and near-direct exposure to flames.

Casa Manyana is rated to withstand near-direct exposure to bushfire flames and be assembled in two weeks. (ABC Illawarra: Charles Rushforth)

With a flat-pack design that fits in the tray of a ute, Mr Pupilli has seen the frame of the building assembled in a single day and estimates the entire build could be completed in two weeks.

This allows Casa Manyana to be classified as temporary emergency accommodation, allowing residents impacted by disaster to immediately start building.

Under NSW planning laws, a development application for temporary emergency accommodation projects on residential land is not needed for two years.

Ranging between $75,000 and $120,000, Casa Manyana was designed by Mr Pupilli to be an affordable option for those rebuilding after a disaster.

"It was this idea of, like, if we did lose our house, how would we get back on the land?" he said.

"That's an important part of the healing process. It would really benefit people to have something delivered flat-pack and be able to put it together in a relatively short time in recovering after a bushfire.

"We also saw it as something that could become part of the permanent dwelling over time."

With the bushfire season currently underway across the local government area, Ms Logge said the prototype version near their home in Manyana had already provided relief.

"We're starting to get some really hot days. I've already been like, 'What should I pop in from the house that can go into Casa Manyana to be protected?'" Ms Logge said.

The project was nominated for two 2026 Houses Awards for both the small project and sustainability categories.

RFS urges residents to prepare for bushfire

Manyana is part of the Shoalhaven local government area, where the Rural Fire Service (RFS) estimates 90 per cent of residents live on bushfire-prone land.

Acting RFS district commander Superintendent David Bartlett said that while the rise of fire-resistant building materials was promising, people could not rely on the design of the house to save them from a bushfire.

David Bartlett says no home is survivable in catastrophic fire conditions. (ABC Illawarra: Charles Rushforth)

"We don't want people to become complacent with the fact that they've constructed a dwelling that they may think is fairly well prepared for fire," he said.

"On a catastrophic fire day, the message from us is that even a well-prepared property is probably not going to be survivable.

"Have you experienced what it's like to be in a very large uncontrolled wildfire? A lot of people don't really know until they're in that situation. That's why we say that it's probably best not to be in that situation in the first place."

This weekend, RFS brigades across the state are hosting public events as part of Get Ready Weekend to help residents prepare for the upcoming bushfire season.

With the likelihood of bushfires increasing across the country this year due to a heightened El Niño, Ms Logge said her family had decided to evacuate early in the event of a bushfire.

The aftermath of a fire in Bendalong in early January 2020, near Manyana. (ABC Illawarra: Jake Lapham)

While the terrifying scenes of smoke and fire were never far from her mind, she said the enduring power of community gave her faith that they could meet whatever challenges the season brought this year.

"The way the community was there for each other was pretty incredible … the human spirit is amazing," she said.

" It makes you feel a bit more brave and less alone. "

World.title: NT paramedics could carry pepper spray for safety, minister says
World.content:
The Northern Territory government has suggested ambulance officers carry pepper spray and body-worn cameras in an effort to combat violent incidents on the job.

St John Ambulance NT said paramedics in Central Australia have faced 88 instances of serious violence since January this year, while first responders in Darwin say there have been record rates of assault.

The Alice Springs Member for Braitling Joshua Burgoyne said it was "extraordinarily disappointing" to see people attack paramedics and that his government was looking at how it could better support the service and its staff.

Josh Burgoyne says he's been speaking with ambulance management about paramedics being offered the option to carry pepper spray to protect themselves. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"There's been conversations obviously with management about whether or not paramedics carrying pepper spray for a defensive aspect is something that they want to do," Mr Burgoyne said.

"Obviously there's going to be mixed views right across the workforce as to whether or not this is a positive thing.

"As a government what we're trying to do is say 'whatever you need it's on the table'."

Pepper or "oleoresin capsicum" spray can be used as a weapon to disarm someone. (ABC News: Daryna Zadvirna)

While St John are yet to respond to questions about whether they will consider introducing pepper spray, NT Shadow Health Minister Chansey Paech said he'll support paramedics in any decision they make.

But he said the government needs to address the root causes of the issue and not rely on band-aid solutions.

"Something that we're all trying to understand here is what's driving this level of aggression and anger towards people who are trying to help in our community, " he said.

"What we're not seeing is how we stop that. We're just grabbing another tool and saying, 'try this, try that'. When we're seeing this behaviour get worse and get worse."

Chansey Paech says he'll support paramedics in any decision they make but other solutions should be investigated. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Mr Paech said he would like to see other approaches considered, including a model involving Aboriginal community police or liaison officers travelling out with ambos.

Earlier this year, St John Ambulance NT said it was considering introducing body-worn cameras following rioting in Alice Springs and ongoing assaults across the NT.

A string of violent incidents

The government floated the pepper spray idea following a string of violent incidents in Central Australia in the past week.

On Friday September 11, six paramedics were forced to barricade themselves inside a home while treating a patient in the Alice Springs eastern suburb of Larapinta.

St John Ambulance NT southern regional manager Abbey Studley told ABC Radio Alice Springs paramedics were tending to the patient when "a large number of people arrived in a taxi" and "the scene changed really quickly".

St John Ambulance NT has long displayed signs on its vehicles reminding people to stay "hands off" with paramedics. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"We went from a critically unwell patient that we were providing rapid life-saving treatment, to all the crew involved having to stand up really rapidly and think about their own safety first," Ms Studley said.

"Our crews basically had to push violent persons outside the house and barricade themselves inside using their bodies and using a stretcher and lock themselves in the house.

"We were unable to care for the patient in the typical fashion because we had to care for our own safety and the crew's safety at that moment.

"We were trying really rapidly to provide that life-saving care, we had to adapt that because of the situation of violence, which was just horrendous."

The team set off duress alarms to notify police they needed urgent back up.

The patient was able to be taken to hospital once officers arrived and the situation was under control.

During one incident St John Ambulance NT staff had to barricade themselves in an Alice Springs home until police arrived. (ABC News: Pete Garnish )

St John Ambulance said the day before that incident a paramedic was struck by a glass bottle that was thrown at them and in a separate incident that week ambulance officers faced threats while transporting a patient.

"We haven't seen a reduction in the statistics around the number of assaults perpetrated across the Northern Territory," Ms Studley said.

"When that happens, once a week, once a shift, every day for a month, and it happens to you and your colleagues, it's really hard for that cumulative effect to not start to ... have an impact on our staff and therefore their welfare."

NT paramedics assaulted, lacking resources The ABC rode along with St John Ambulance NT paramedics to hear the impact under-resourcing is having on the workforce, including stories of staff being assaulted on the job.

As a result, St John Ambulance has rolled out additional training in preventative action, de-escalation, cultural safety and have introduced a policy encouraging staff to withdraw when they feel unsafe.

"Because of violence perpetrated by others on scene, our crews are having to withdraw and that takes a toll on, not only the critically ill patient, but also on the paramedics who joined this career to really help people," Ms Studley said.

"It's really disappointing, but it's also the decision that I really champion for my staff is you come first and I need to be able to put you guys on the road every day.

"And if you're not safe, you can't deliver that care anyway."

World.title: Live: Qantas seeks to avert freight ground crew strikes
World.content:
Qantas is expected to head to the Fair Work Commission this morning in a bid to stop ground crews walking off the job next week.

Hundreds of Qantas Ground Services workers have voted in favour of protected industrial action. According to the Transport Workers Union, the action includes 24-hour stoppages in Victoria on Wednesday, and across the rest of the country on Thursday.

The agreement covers around 650 employees, with the majority working in Qantas Freight.

A smaller group services QantasLink regional flights at Sydney Airport.

The workers do not service Qantas' mainline domestic or international flights, or QantasLink services at other airports.

“Workers do not take this action lightly. Any disruption to freight, including Australia Post shipments, sits solely at the feet of Qantas management and its brutal disregard for customers and the workforce,” TWU national secretary Michael Kaine said.

“We remain committed to reaching an agreement with our Qantas Ground Services employees that includes annual pay rises for our people,” a Qantas spokesperson said.

They added there are contingency plans to minimise any impact on customers.

The ABC has also contacted Australia Post for comment this morning.

Abuja, Nigeria: At least 33 suspects arrested for alleged illegal mining were found dead in Nigerian security custody, officials said, pointing to a suspected disease outbreak in the area.

The detainees died in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps, or NSCDC, in north-central Niger state, its spokesman Abubakar Muti said.

They had been in detention since the security agency carried out arrests on Tuesday and Wednesday over suspicion of illegal mining in the state, the NSCDC said.

While the agency suspects a disease, the detainees’ bodies had been sent to a local hospital for “further medical examination to establish the actual cause of death”, a spokesman said.

A Queensland teen allegedly operated several social media accounts to post extremist material that supported violence against migrants and people of both Islamic and Jewish faith.

Federal investigators say they were tipped off by the FBI about an Australian who was posting extremist content on social media advocating for violence and referencing terrorist attacks, leading to the teen’s arrest.

Police raided a home in Warner, north of Brisbane, in May and seized several devices they will allege were used to commit the crimes.

Declan John Stout, 18, was charged with 28 offences related to posting extremist material online, one count of using a carriage service to menace or harass, and one count of possessing child abuse material.

He has been remanded in custody since May 27, and will face a Pine Rivers Magistrate on Friday.
