World.title: How an NBA legend’s ‘superpower’ has shaped Melbourne United’s new coach
World.content:
SportBasketballNBL How an NBA legend’s ‘superpower’ has shaped Melbourne United’s new coach Jon Pierik September 18, 2026 — 8:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When it comes to coaching, there have been few better in NBA history than San Antonio Spurs legend Gregg Popovich. “Pop”, as he is affectionately known, won five NBA titles – the last in 2014 – with the legendary Tim Duncan as his on-court pilot, and Australian great Patty Mills sharing in that final victory lap. So, when it came to the opportunity to lean into Popovich’s so-called “superpower”, new Melbourne United coach Jacob Chance was all ears. Here’s how we do it: Melbourne United coach Jacob Chance helped lead his club to the NBL Blitz title in Bendigo this month. Getty Images for NBL Chance was coaching the Spurs’ G League affiliate, the Austin Spurs, this year when Popovich – no longer coaching but still a key, even mystical, figure – visited the change room.



“He spoke to our team before one of the games. He also spoke to the main team before the play-offs,” Chance said of the San Antonio Spurs, who returned to the NBA Finals under new coach Mitch Johnson, falling to the New York Knicks. Related Article NBL ‘Have you not seen what I have made?’ Why Joe Ingles gave up $5.1 million to play in the NBL “You hear different things, but again, I think his superpower is just how clear he keeps it with the expectations of what it means to be a Spur, and it really just comes back to that – play really hard, play the right way, and be really coachable and a great teammate – and he just holds them to account for that.” Basketball can be turned into complex game of strategy, but Chance, just 32 and the youngest head coach in the NBL since Shawn Dennis led the now defunct Newcastle Falcons in 1997, has the ability to simplify in-depth analysis, ensuring players and fellow coaches understand what’s needed. It’s not hard to see why United owners Travis Knipe and Aaron Sansoni, and chief executive Nick Truelson, hold Chance in such high esteem, and legendary coach Brian Goorjian describes him as “elite”.



“It was good and refreshing to see. Like, yeah, as much as this is the most heightened sense of basketball in the world, you know, [the] NBA Finals, you’re still talking about the same things,” Chance said of Popovich’s chat to the NBA Spurs. The Spurs Way: Legendary NBA coach Gregg Popovich has had an influence on new Melbourne United coach Jacob Chance. Getty Images “Everyone asked me when I was over there, like, ‘What have you learnt coming over here?’ “It’s the same way you lose basketball games in under-10 Perth games – your Perth girls’ game you’re coaching, or another under-14 boys game in Melbourne you’re coaching, or the Spurs in the NBA Finals or Melbourne United – you will lose for the same reasons. You didn’t get back in transition. You didn’t help each other. You didn’t play the right way. You didn’t play hard enough, and so it was just refreshing to be on the biggest stage, yet we’re still talking about the same thing ... [It was] a good learning moment for me.” ‘I think his superpower is just how clear he keeps it with the expectations of what it means to be a Spur ... play really hard, play the right way, and be really coachable and a great teammate.’ United coach Jacob Chance on NBA legend Gregg Popovich



Chance’s mantra of “playing the right way” was also reinforced through watching Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama, and the way he prepares, searching for that “one per cent improvement”. “The talent’s one thing, but just his demeanour and how he approaches the game is pretty special,” Chance said, chatting in his office at Hoops City in Cheltenham. Related Article NBA Giddey leaks: Bulls superstar breaks the news of gun NBL recruit “Like today, for example, we finish practice at 1 o’clock in the afternoon. We don’t practice again until 10 o’clock on Thursday morning. What are you doing between now and then? “I think [with] Vic [Wembanyama], the curiosity and the willingness he shows to try and find ways to improve his body and use that time well, I think it really separates him from other guys, so it’s a good one for us.”



Chance, a Perth native, has taken these “learnings” to United, the famous “Spurs Way” clearly strong in his thinking, and even in sight, with Brett Brown, the former NBL championship and Boomers coach and long-time Spurs assistant, dropping by training last month. The chance to replace three-time NBL championship coach Dean Vickerman as head coach of a marquee NBL club was too good to refuse for Chance, who initially rejected United’s advances before club chiefs circled back with a bigger offer, including the role of head of basketball operations. Ready to go: NBA veteran Joe Ingles and fellow United recruit Sam Waardenburg were a part of United’s off-season rebuild. Eddie Jim Having progressed as a highly respected assistant alongside Trevor Gleeson in Perth, beginning with the Wildcats as an intern in the video room, before joining Scott Roth in Tasmania, then Vickerman at United, and becoming a deputy head coach with the Boomers, Chance, complete with a four-year contract, and fiancée Bree opted to return to Melbourne. Bree, however, has yet to arrive, the couple having welcomed Beaux, an Aussie Shepherd, into their home before the opportunity to return to Melbourne was presented. Beaux needs to pass testing and quarantine measures before being allowed to get on a plane, and that won’t happen until closer to Christmas.



“It’s a nasty little process, but it’s worth it once we get everyone here,” Chance said. Meanwhile, there is plenty of work for Chance to do, beginning with the home opener against six-time league most valuable player Bryce Cotton and the Adelaide 36ers on Saturday night. United have built a championship-level roster – former NBA players Joe Ingles, Cole Anthony, Luke Travers and Josh Oduro joining blue-chip New Zealand big man Sam Waardenburg (from Cairns) in ensuring veteran star Chris Goulding has a chance for another ring. Despite early injury issues, the signs are promising, with United claiming the NBL Blitz pre-season tournament title. Goulding, entering his 12th season with the franchise, said Chance had impressed through building relationships and his game craft.



“I don’t want to say surprised me, but what’s been really great has been his attention to detail, his intent to get clarity, and how steadfast he is in what he believes in, and what he wants us to do and how he thinks we can be successful in that. He’s steadfast in that,” Goulding said. San Antonio Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama. Getty Images Ingles, the NBA and Boomers veteran, is ready after a pre-season calf issue, and has delivered with his intangibles off the court in showing the younger players what is required to succeed at the top level. Anthony, a former teammate of Ingles with the Orlando Magic, will provide speed and shooting. Perth-product Travers, a former Cleveland Cavalier, will again play multiple roles in his return to the club. Oduro was with the New Orleans Pelicans last season, while Waardenburg is an athletic forward who can shoot from outside. Loading

World.title: Only one of the Serong boys will reach the grand final this year. Their mum is already taking sides
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Only one of the Serong boys will reach the grand final this year. Their mum is already taking sides Andrew Wu September 18, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

On Friday night at the SCG, Tania and Jamie Serong and their family will gather in the Fremantle rooms for a presentation in recognition of their son Caleb’s 150th game for the Dockers. They’ll then head in separate directions. While Tania takes her seat in the stands among the Fremantle friends and families’ section, her husband will make his way onto the hallowed turf of the SCG to be part of a guard of honour for Sydney’s players as they run onto the field. Jai and Caleb Serong (right) as kids. If you think Matthew Pavlich, the Fremantle great turned Sydney chief executive, was conflicted, spare a thought for the Serongs, whose sons Caleb and Jai go head-to-head for a grand final berth.



Unlike just about everyone else in the sold-out crowd on Friday night, the Serongs can’t lose, no matter what the result is. But they can’t win either. “I’m really torn,” Jamie told this masthead this week. “No matter how you look at it, you’ll have one extremely happy young boy, and one devastated young boy. It’s going to be a challenge on that front.” Caleb Serong is one of the AFL’s premier midfielders. Getty Images Sibling rivalry in September is not uncommon in the AFL. The Hill brothers, Brad and Stephen for Hawthorn and Fremantle respectively – squared off in the 2013 grand final. Brothers Reid (Sam and Ben) and Shaw (Rhyce and Shaw) met in the preliminary final the year earlier, as did the Selwoods (Joel for Geelong, and Scott and the late Adam for West Coast) in 2011. This will be the third time Caleb and Jai will play against each other at AFL level, but never have the stakes been so high.



The match will be a family reunion of sorts. Almost 20 of them will be there, including the boys’ grandfather and aunt from Mum’s side, Caleb’s wife Chloe and her parents, and Jai’s girlfriend and her sister. View post on X The brothers have dismissed the occasion as just another game, and they’ll treat each other as just another opponent, but it’s not as straightforward for their parents. This has not been an easy week for them. For Tania, there has been an underlying nervousness since it became apparent a fortnight ago the two clubs could meet in a preliminary final. “It’s a wonderful problem to have, but it’s still intense,” Tania said.



Jai Serong has fast become a key component for the Swans, given his versatility in playing a number of roles. Sam Mooy When their boys play, the Serongs have a foot in each camp. Mum will sit with one club, Dad the other. When Fremantle hosted Sydney in July, Jamie watched the game with the Dockers families as he had not seen them for a while, and Tania was with the Swans. They decided then they would swap for the next match-up. While most mothers sit on the fence, Tania’s allegiances are firmly with the Dockers. No, she does not have a favourite son, but as neutrality is difficult for her, she has decided she would be all-in behind the team she is sitting with. The next day, she’ll swap colours and watch the replay from the point of view of the other team, to appreciate the other perspective.



“I’ve tried to watch games as a neutral – you don’t watch anything, you’re off in fairy land, [and] you can’t ground into the game,” Tania said. “It’s really important to watch the game on one side or the other. “You can’t actually barrack for two teams at once. This week, I’m purple.” The exception will be if Jai is lining up for the winning goal after the siren. “I would be with the one kicking – that’s a special moment,” Tania said. “If you have the opportunity, take it.” Tania, though, won’t be wearing the Fremantle colours, nor will the couple be putting on split scarves. That drew too many weird looks, she said. Instead, she will wear a badge for both sons, one on each side, as her show of support.



Jame and Tania Serong will have their allegiances split on Friday night. Usually, when only one son is playing, Tania takes her eye off the ball to keep watch on him. When the two clubs last met – and she was sitting with the Swans – she did not know where Caleb was until he had the ball. “A couple of times I checked what his stats were like to keep an eye on how he was going,” Tania said. ‘You can’t actually barrack for two teams at once. This week, I’m purple.’ Caleb and Jai Serong’s mum, Tania Jamie has a different approach. Earlier this year, he found himself applauding Fremantle more, only because they scored more in a come-from-behind victory.



“I do have a real weird feeling, it’s not how much I support but how much I don’t get angry,” Jamie said. “I can get frustrated if the opposition’s winning. Last week, I was holding my breath for a quarter and a half. I don’t get as stressed because the opposition I have a lot of love for.” Jai has played primarily on the wing but, after the late-season upheaval in the Swans team, spent much of the qualifying final in the centre square, which is Caleb’s natural habitat. Even if Jai is not given the job of shadowing his brother, they will undoubtedly draw swords at some point. As kids, the pair, separated by two years and seven days, were fierce competitors. Throw in youngest brother Liam, a talented footballer himself in the VFL and at local level, and there was little peace for mum and dad.



“Cricket was the worst,” Tania said. “You’d think, ‘Oh good, they’re playing cricket’, then within an over, someone had cracked it, someone wasn’t out. It was all very competitive. “There were lots of fights. They’d get physical. You’d have to react quickly. Otherwise it would escalate pretty quickly. I just herded them to different places. It was full on, it was very busy.” View post on X For much of their childhoods, Caleb had the size advantage until he reached 15, when Jai had a growth spurt. Caleb is now listed at 180 centimetres, 13cm shorter than Jai. For competitive siblings, having a taller younger brother adds complexities at that age. “As you can imagine, everyone else had a comment on it,” Tania said. “‘Oh your brother is getting taller than you’.”



Jai, both parents say, would not often stir up his brother, but when he did, he would make it count. Related Article AFL 2026 AFL preliminary final teams and expert tips: Skipper’s replacement named; Lions make a key call “Jai would say stuff like, ‘What’s it like down there?’,” Jamie said. In the main, Caleb had come to terms with his lot though he would occasionally wonder why he had missed out on that part of the genetic lottery. “I honestly think Caleb was hoping there was more growth coming,” Jamie said. “I must admit there would be the odd time when Jai passed him, there’d be only me and Tania around, and he’d look at us and go, ‘What the hell happened? Where’s my height?’



“Caleb didn’t mind. I suppose he’d talk it off and come up with some other way he was better than Jai.” As footballers, their careers have taken different paths. Caleb was a top-10 draft pick who played just about immediately, has multiple All-Australian and best-and-fairest awards. Jai, a late selection, has fought tooth and nail for his 33 games, moving to a second club for greater opportunities. They have played plenty of cricket together, but the only times they have been on the same footy field have been as opponents. They could easily have been teammates. Hawthorn selected Jai with pick 53 in 2021. Fremantle had pick 54. Jamie got a call after the draft from Dockers coach Justin Longmuir, chief executive Simon Garlick and then footy boss Peter Bell apologising, telling him they would have taken him with the next selection. “Jai would say stuff like, ‘What’s it like down there?’” Jamie Serong on a rare sledge from Jai to his older, “little” brother Caleb



The Dockers were rebuffed again last year when Jai, coming off back-to-back best and fairests with Hawthorn’s VFL team Box Hill, chose to head north rather than west. Mum, Dad and older brother would have loved to see Jai don the purple with Caleb, but understood the decision. Editor's pick AFL 2026 Depleted, doubted and written off, yet somehow the Swans are just one win from another grand final “We were proud,” Jamie said. “He didn’t get selfish but thought about where he fit the best and what gave him the best opportunity to succeed. “You did think to yourself if they were both in the one place, you know the brothers would like to play together. Once again, Caleb was great with that. He knew why Jai did it and was totally happy for him.” For the parents, it would have eased the logistical challenges that come with supporting three sons who play football in three states, sometimes at the same time.



They do not get to many games together, outside of the rare occasions the Dockers play in Melbourne. In a normal year, Tania would travel to Perth about five times, preferably during a point in the season when the Dockers play at home on consecutive weeks so she can spend more time with her son. But this has not been a normal year for the family. In February, Jamie was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma. He’s happy to for his health battle to be made public as long as it does not overshadow his boys’ achievements. He has finished chemotherapy with radiation therapy to come. The illness has made it challenging to fly interstate too often for games, Jamie said. Travel will not be an issue for them in grand final week, barring injury or suspension to the winning brother.

World.title: ASX set to rise, Wall Street climbs as oil prices slide, bond market pressure eases; UK keeps rates on hold
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, Wall Street climbs as oil prices slide, bond market pressure eases; UK keeps rates on hold Stan Choe Updated September 18, 2026 — 6:25am ,first published 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market rallied to its best day in six weeks after falling oil prices and easing pressure from the bond market helped Wall Street reverse many of its moves from the prior day. The S&P 500 jumped 1.1 per cent for just its second rise in the last nine days. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 316 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.7 per cent. Wall Street’s benchmark index is on track for just its second gain in the last nine sessions. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 4.57am AEST pointing to a gain of 57 points, or 0.7 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.4 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US71.11¢. US stocks got a boost after the price for a barrel of Brent crude oil slid 1 per cent to settle at $US104.82. That’s down from the nearly $US110 it reached earlier in the week on worries that the war with Iran will keep oil bottled up in the Middle East instead of going to customers worldwide.



Brent is of course still much more expensive than the $US72 per barrel that it cost earlier this summer, but Thursday’s drop helped pull yields lower in the bond market and removed some pressure on stocks. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93 per cent from 5.01 per cent late Wednesday. Related Article Aviation Qantas ground staff set to strike over ‘Joyce-era’ bargaining agreements Higher yields make it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, from the US government to people looking to buy houses to businesses wanting to build data centers. That in turn slows the economy. The Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised the short-term interest rate that it controls, the federal funds rate, by a quarter of a percentage point for its first hike in more than three years. Officials also signalled they may raise the federal funds rate one more time this year as they try to get the nation’s high inflation under control. The signals sent Wall Street on a roller coaster. Stocks initially remained higher for the day after the Fed made its announcement Wednesday. They then slid sharply before recovering a chunk of the losses before trading ended.



On the upside for markets, the shift to higher interest rates built confidence that the Fed is committed to getting inflation back to its target of 2 per cent. Questions had begun to bubble earlier about whether it would feel pressure from President Donald Trump, who is calling for lower interest rates. And the short-term cost of pain for the economy could be worth it if it gets inflation under control following years of its staying too high. On the downside for markets, higher rates undercut prices for stocks and other investments. When investors earn more in interest from bonds, which are considered safer investments, they’re less willing to pay high prices for other investments. That’s beyond the slowing effect that higher rates have on the economy in hopes of removing fuel for inflation. Some reports on Thursday signalled the US economy may be strong enough to withstand higher interest rates. One said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week. Another said that manufacturing growth in the mid-Atlantic region was stronger than economists expected. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday that a strengthening economy is one of the reasons Fed officials moved to raise interest rates after keeping them on hold earlier this year. He also cited “geopolitics,” along with the threat that the increases in prices it’s causing could filter out and push up inflation elsewhere. That’s likely a nod to the war with Iran and its effect on oil prices.



On Wall Street, stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry continued to rebound following their worldwide slide on Monday. Nvidia climbed 2.5 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices rose 6.4 per cent. That was even though OpenAI disclosed six more reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in AI models. Leaders of the AI industry over the weekend called for a slowdown in development to address safety issues for humanity Stocks of several homebuilders also rose, even though a report showed the industry broke ground on fewer new homes last month than economists expected. The housing industry has been one of the hardest hit by the climb for the 10-year Treasury’s yield, which topped 5 per cent this week for the first time since 2023 and has pulled mortgage rates higher. Thursday’s ease in yields helped D.R. Horton rise 1.5 per cent, while PulteGroup added 1.1 per cent. Rival Lennar erased an early loss and climbed 1.7 per cent after reporting weaker profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. All told, the S&P 500 rose 85.95 points to 7,637.76. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 316.14 to 51,778.04, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 439.87 to 26,418.30.

World.title: ‘Like a lottery winner’: Charles ‘elated’ after Diana’s death, her brother’s new book claims
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family ‘Like a lottery winner’: Charles ‘elated’ after Diana’s death, her brother’s new book claims Sam Tobin September 18, 2026 — 6:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: King Charles sounded “like a lottery winner” after the death of his late first wife Diana, her brother writes in his forthcoming book, according to newly published extracts. Diana’s brother Earl Spencer said the then-prince Charles seemed “giddily elated” in the immediate aftermath of Diana’s death in 1997, possibly because he felt it meant he was freer to marry again, according to passages in the Daily Mail. Loading Charles on Wednesday took the unusual step of responding to criticism after the first extracts of Spencer’s book were published, saying via a spokesperson that grief could impact reason, judgment and memory. There was no new comment from the King on the latest excerpts, which also stated that Diana went to a site of many suicides on Britain’s south coast, but that her love for her sons, William and Harry, “stopped her from going further”.



“It is a sad fact that, in her later years, Diana drove herself more than once to Beachy Head, the highest chalk sea cliff in England, while contemplating ending it all,” Spencer wrote. Diana was killed at the age of 36 when the car carrying her and her lover Dodi al-Fayed crashed in Paris as it sped away from chasing paparazzi photographers on motorbikes. Prince Charles and Princess Diana on their tour to Australia in 1985. AP Earl Spencer (centre) is greeted by his nephews, Harry and William, at Kensington Palace in London in 2021. AP Spencer says in the book – Swan Song: Diana, My Sister – that he spoke to Charles shortly after Diana’s death was confirmed, writing: “Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated – like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time.”



Spencer added: “Looking back now, I suspect the prince’s first reaction must have been to think more of how this event might free him to marry the woman he loved, rather than appreciating the loss of one he did not.” Related Article Royal family ‘We’ll forget her soon enough’: Diana’s brother makes explosive claim about Charles Charles and Diana separated in 1992 and divorced in 1996. That was a year after Diana told the BBC that “there were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded”, in reference to Charles’ relationship with Camilla Parker Bowles, whom he married in 2005. Buckingham Palace took the rare step on Wednesday (UK time) of rebutting an explosive claim in the book that Charles said people would forget Diana “soon enough” after her death. A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”



Swan Song: Diana, My Sister by Earl Spencer. That claim centred on the earl’s strong belief that Diana would not have wanted William and Harry to walk behind her coffin in her funeral procession, but that Charles insisted the plan go ahead. “He unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death,” the earl wrote. “‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough’.” Julian Payne, the now-King’s former communications secretary, on Thursday said Charles told staff never to criticise Diana in the years after her death. Payne, who worked alongside Charles during the 20th anniversary of Diana’s death in 2017, told the BBC that he did not recognise “the way the King is being characterised in those remarks”.



“What I remember was he was very clear that there was never to be any criticism, never to be any pushback on the narratives that were usually highly critical of him,” he said. “He was absolutely emphatic that we were to respect her memory and not undermine it in any way. When he was telling us there was never to be any criticism or pushback, that wasn’t about him. Harry (left) poses with former soldiers as he arrives at the Invictus Spirit Awards in London on Thursday. AP “That was absolutely about the late princess and her memory, so it seems to me very odd that in the moment itself, with the grief of his family and his own shock, that he would choose that moment to use those words. It’s just not language that I recognise.” Spencer’s claims appears likely to heighten the rifts within the family. Prince Harry has a strained relationship with his father after his memoir, Spare, which also touched on the decision over the funeral.



Harry, meanwhile, made his first public appearance on Thursday (London time) since he and his wife, Meghan, returned to Britain after six years in California, speaking at a charity event and attending an awards ceremony in London. Related Article AI King warns AI leaders of ‘existential dangers’ if tech falls into wrong hands Harry, Meghan and their children Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, relocated last month – surprising even their close family. The Duke of Sussex attended the inaugural Invictus Spirit Awards in London, which are linked to the Invictus Games, the sporting competition he founded for wounded, injured and sick military veterans. Earlier, he spoke at an event focused on improving the care of children wounded in conflict hosted by charity Save the Children and Imperial College London.

World.title: Larissa Lambert, Australia’s empress of R&B, is ready for her close-up
World.content:
Larissa Lambert: “You’ve just got to get to a place of not giving a f---, and that’s when it all flows out.”

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If R&B has been perennially overlooked in Australia, Larissa Lambert has been its best-kept secret. The 30-year-old has a voice so warm and vibrant it could melt your butter, fry your pancakes, boil your coffee – the full breakfast. It’s the kind of thing a religious person might call “a gift from God”. When did she know she had it? “This is so cliche but, honestly, I knew since I could f---ing talk,” Lambert says with all the bluntness that’s made her a social media favourite. “I have memories of my family and people at school sitting around me being like, ‘do it again!’, and I’d sing a line and they’d be like, ‘whoa!’ So I knew, like, ‘I’m good at this’. There was no doubt about it. I had no plan B. I was like, ‘I’m gonna be a singer’.” More than a decade into her career, with viral successes and plaudits from superstars like SZA and Justin Bieber to her name, she’s finally releasing her long-awaited debut album, Yearning. Filled with her effortless vocals, production flourishes that flitter between Y2K nostalgia and club trends, and writing that coolly probes her desires and insecurities, the album is a cohesive triumph. It begs the question: why did it take so long? “I just never felt like I was ready,” says Lambert. “I was always like, ‘people are expecting so much from me’, so it needed to feel authentic. It needed to be me.” Wearing black leather pants, her pierced septum gleaming, Lambert looks every bit the star as we speak in a room the size of a confessional in Virgin Music’s offices in inner-Sydney’s Chippendale. We’re barely 10 minutes into the interview when she begins to outline the harrowing challenges that, at least partly, skewered the timeline to her debut. Three years ago, Lambert suffered psychosis following withdrawals from an addiction to prescription Valium. “My brain basically just went f---ing haywire. It took me a whole year to get back to normal,” she says. “During a psychosis, your whole world is flipped. I just felt hopeless. It’s f---ing scary.



“It’s like a panic attack on steroids. Everyone’s different with how they experience psychosis; some people can be aware they’re in it and some people can completely black out. I understood what was going on but you’re in an intense state of paranoia, you have intrusive thoughts, your moods are up and down. Writing was the only thing that was keeping me sane.” She’d been through drug psychosis before, years prior when she was 22. “That was from an edible, actually, because even marijuana is a big trigger for psychosis. If your family has a history of mental health issues you should never touch it,” she says. She’s more protective of herself now. “No substances, I’m 100 per cent sober,” she says. “I used to have a very addictive personality and I couldn’t say no, couldn’t turn down the party phase. Growing up, it was always like that. “The music industry, artists, creatives – we’re so addicted to escapism, especially if you come from not the best upbringing. You tend to emotionally regulate through substances. In my case, that’s what it was. I never knew how to deal with my emotions, so I would smoke to get out of them or take some sleepers to mellow out. “It’s so toxic, man, and it catches up to you. It caught up to me. So I’m 100 per cent sober, straighty-180 now. Maybe a little sip of wine here and there, but otherwise … I can’t, it’s not worth it.” Lambert had been working at a pizza shop in her home town, Rio Bravo in Ballarat – “incredible pizza, one of my favourite jobs I ever had” – when she scored her first break. At 16, a scout from The X Factor, then airing on the Seven Network, phoned, inviting her to an artist development camp after seeing videos she’d posted on Facebook of herself singing on her bedroom floor. “I thought it was a scam,” Lambert recalls. “He was like, ‘we’ve got this camp, it’s $500’. I was like, you’re f---ing joking.” After verifying the call was legit, she used funds she’d been saving to buy a laptop to accept the offer. Her boss at the pizza shop paid for her flights to Sydney. “He was a blessing,” says Lambert. At the camp, she was successfully recruited into the girl group Paris Inc.



“It was fun. It felt like training,” Lambert recalls of her time on The X Factor. “I needed it for my confidence. I used to be really, like, inwards. Being in the girl group helped me come out of my shell.” In 2019, after Paris Inc split, Lambert received interest from the States; a girl who was working with R&B star Jeremih – famed for his DJ Mustard-produced smash Don’t Tell ’Em, still a barbershop staple – found her on Instagram and pitched her to the singer. “He took me under his wing,” says Lambert. “He mentored me about how the States works, the culture, the people, certain flows and how to add more pockets to my songs. I’m so grateful for him. He wanted to sign me at the time but I ended up turning it down because I wanted to stay independent.” Larissa Lambert’s debut album, Yearning, has been a long time coming. Even now, Lambert remains an independent artist. She must’ve had major labels chasing her for ages? “Oh yeah, I’ve had an offer from pretty much every single label, but it’s always just been a standard label deal,” she says. What does that mean? “It means they’ll give you a label deal out of the 1980s where there’s nothing – literally, less than minus – in your favour,” she says, laughing. Her current arrangement with Virgin Music is a distribution deal, where she owns her masters and licenses them to the label for a set period. “Virgin were the only label that respected me, understood the vision and listened,” Lambert explains. “With a lot of the major labels, you’re just another TikTok viral sensation they’re gonna sign, and if you pop off, you pop off. I feel like labels have lost the art of developing an artist.” When labels approached her in the past, being a young artist, how did she know the deals weren’t in her best interests? “My intuition, I guess. It just never felt right.”



She pauses and recalibrates. “Actually, you know what it was? It’s because I went viral before I ever signed anything, so I started seeing my cheques!” she says with a laugh. “And knowing that a label would take 80 per cent of my earnings just to say they have me but not do anything for me? I was like, that is stupid, you’re not taking my money!” Back in 2021, a cover she sang of SWV’s Weak went “stupid viral” on TikTok. “Someone from the Philippines, and Indonesia as well, they started a dance trend to it. All these different trends took off. It was like a tree branch. It just kept going.” Lambert once said the viral cover made her “a lot of money”, enough to keep her career going. How so? “Well, I dropped the full cover on Spotify and then, you know, you make money from the master percentage. But then all the publishing obviously goes to SWV. So they made a good chunk off me, too!” She’d lucked into the exact kind of virality record labels employ entire departments to manufacture. “Yeah, and you can’t,” says Lambert. “You can definitely make a song viral if you put millions of dollars into it but is it gonna stick, though? Authentic viral is so special but no one knows the f---ing recipe. If I did, I’d go viral every time.” The experience gave her a unique insight into industry machinations, which was significant when record labels came calling. “They literally take 80 per cent of your earnings – it’s crazy! Like, how are you supposed to live? Off a tiny advance that’s supposed to last you three years? It doesn’t make sense. In my opinion, if you’re an artist and you sign to a label, you shouldn’t be working a nine-to-five. You should be able to put all your time and focus on your music and have an advance that will last you,” she says. “But, like, it’s a risk on both sides because labels are also risking a lot of money on certain artists, so I get it. But that’s why I chose to stay independent with a distro deal, and I vouch for that for any up-and-coming artists as well. It’s good because it forces you to learn every angle, so you’re never getting taken advantage of.”



On social media, Lambert’s gift has earned praise from SZA, Bieber and Ty Dolla $ign, a case of game recognising game. Do such co-signs translate into anything tangible? “Like, does it bring people to me?” Lambert asks. “Oh, of course. Especially when they’ve shared my stuff, they put on so many new listeners. But just having the recognition from them is crazy. The fact that my idols are seeing me and appreciating me? It’s a huge pat on the back to let me know I’m doing something right.” It makes it even more intriguing that she didn’t release her debut album sooner. Any other young artist would’ve been convinced to capitalise on the moment while there’s heat. “I know, I look back and I wonder if I could have, but I don’t think it would have worked,” says Lambert. The key to unlocking her album, she says, was linking up with executive producer Khaled Rohaim. Rohaim – a Grammy-nominated Sydney producer who has worked with stars including Rihanna, Doja Cat and The Kid Laroi – had long had Lambert in his sights. “He was trying to get me to leave the girl group when I was 17 and I was like, ‘who is this guy?’,” Lambert says, laughing. “I had no idea what he’d done but he actually has some of the most insane credits. Eventually I ended up doing a session with him three years ago, and we’ve been inseparable ever since.” The album’s emotional through line lies in its title. “Yearning” is a term that has had a cultural blow-up this year, a buzzword that’s defined a generation’s pushback against the casual nonchalance of online dating. It’s also long been the central emotion in R&B, from Jodeci’s Feenin’ to Kehlani’s Folded. “It’s about letting go of ego, bringing back authenticity and longing and openness,” says Lambert of her album’s message. “We’re in such a culture of being independent and being within yourself, and it’s toxic because we’re not meant to be like that. It makes people go insane and get depressed.”

Abuja, Nigeria: At least 33 suspects arrested for alleged illegal mining were found dead in Nigerian security custody, officials said, pointing to a suspected disease outbreak in the area.

The detainees died in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defense Corps, or NSCDC, in north-central Niger state, its spokesman Abubakar Muti said.

They had been in detention since the security agency carried out arrests on Tuesday and Wednesday over suspicion of illegal mining in the state, the NSCDC said.

While the agency suspects a disease, the detainees’ bodies had been sent to a local hospital for “further medical examination to establish the actual cause of death”, a spokesman said.

World.title: How an NBA legend’s ‘superpower’ has shaped Melbourne United’s new coach
World.content:
SportBasketballNBL How an NBA legend’s ‘superpower’ has shaped Melbourne United’s new coach Jon Pierik September 18, 2026 — 8:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When it comes to coaching, there have been few better in NBA history than San Antonio Spurs legend Gregg Popovich. “Pop”, as he is affectionately known, won five NBA titles – the last in 2014 – with the legendary Tim Duncan as his on-court pilot, and Australian great Patty Mills sharing in that final victory lap. So, when it came to the opportunity to lean into Popovich’s so-called “superpower”, new Melbourne United coach Jacob Chance was all ears. Here’s how we do it: Melbourne United coach Jacob Chance helped lead his club to the NBL Blitz title in Bendigo this month. Getty Images for NBL Chance was coaching the Spurs’ G League affiliate, the Austin Spurs, this year when Popovich – no longer coaching but still a key, even mystical, figure – visited the change room.



“He spoke to our team before one of the games. He also spoke to the main team before the play-offs,” Chance said of the San Antonio Spurs, who returned to the NBA Finals under new coach Mitch Johnson, falling to the New York Knicks. Related Article NBL ‘Have you not seen what I have made?’ Why Joe Ingles gave up $5.1 million to play in the NBL “You hear different things, but again, I think his superpower is just how clear he keeps it with the expectations of what it means to be a Spur, and it really just comes back to that – play really hard, play the right way, and be really coachable and a great teammate – and he just holds them to account for that.” Basketball can be turned into complex game of strategy, but Chance, just 32 and the youngest head coach in the NBL since Shawn Dennis led the now defunct Newcastle Falcons in 1997, has the ability to simplify in-depth analysis, ensuring players and fellow coaches understand what’s needed. It’s not hard to see why United owners Travis Knipe and Aaron Sansoni, and chief executive Nick Truelson, hold Chance in such high esteem, and legendary coach Brian Goorjian describes him as “elite”.



“It was good and refreshing to see. Like, yeah, as much as this is the most heightened sense of basketball in the world, you know, [the] NBA Finals, you’re still talking about the same things,” Chance said of Popovich’s chat to the NBA Spurs. The Spurs Way: Legendary NBA coach Gregg Popovich has had an influence on new Melbourne United coach Jacob Chance. Getty Images “Everyone asked me when I was over there, like, ‘What have you learnt coming over here?’ “It’s the same way you lose basketball games in under-10 Perth games – your Perth girls’ game you’re coaching, or another under-14 boys game in Melbourne you’re coaching, or the Spurs in the NBA Finals or Melbourne United – you will lose for the same reasons. You didn’t get back in transition. You didn’t help each other. You didn’t play the right way. You didn’t play hard enough, and so it was just refreshing to be on the biggest stage, yet we’re still talking about the same thing ... [It was] a good learning moment for me.” ‘I think his superpower is just how clear he keeps it with the expectations of what it means to be a Spur ... play really hard, play the right way, and be really coachable and a great teammate.’ United coach Jacob Chance on NBA legend Gregg Popovich



Chance’s mantra of “playing the right way” was also reinforced through watching Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama, and the way he prepares, searching for that “one per cent improvement”. “The talent’s one thing, but just his demeanour and how he approaches the game is pretty special,” Chance said, chatting in his office at Hoops City in Cheltenham. Related Article NBA Giddey leaks: Bulls superstar breaks the news of gun NBL recruit “Like today, for example, we finish practice at 1 o’clock in the afternoon. We don’t practice again until 10 o’clock on Thursday morning. What are you doing between now and then? “I think [with] Vic [Wembanyama], the curiosity and the willingness he shows to try and find ways to improve his body and use that time well, I think it really separates him from other guys, so it’s a good one for us.”



Chance, a Perth native, has taken these “learnings” to United, the famous “Spurs Way” clearly strong in his thinking, and even in sight, with Brett Brown, the former NBL championship and Boomers coach and long-time Spurs assistant, dropping by training last month. The chance to replace three-time NBL championship coach Dean Vickerman as head coach of a marquee NBL club was too good to refuse for Chance, who initially rejected United’s advances before club chiefs circled back with a bigger offer, including the role of head of basketball operations. Ready to go: NBA veteran Joe Ingles and fellow United recruit Sam Waardenburg were a part of United’s off-season rebuild. Eddie Jim Having progressed as a highly respected assistant alongside Trevor Gleeson in Perth, beginning with the Wildcats as an intern in the video room, before joining Scott Roth in Tasmania, then Vickerman at United, and becoming a deputy head coach with the Boomers, Chance, complete with a four-year contract, and fiancée Bree opted to return to Melbourne. Bree, however, has yet to arrive, the couple having welcomed Beaux, an Aussie Shepherd, into their home before the opportunity to return to Melbourne was presented. Beaux needs to pass testing and quarantine measures before being allowed to get on a plane, and that won’t happen until closer to Christmas.



“It’s a nasty little process, but it’s worth it once we get everyone here,” Chance said. Meanwhile, there is plenty of work for Chance to do, beginning with the home opener against six-time league most valuable player Bryce Cotton and the Adelaide 36ers on Saturday night. United have built a championship-level roster – former NBA players Joe Ingles, Cole Anthony, Luke Travers and Josh Oduro joining blue-chip New Zealand big man Sam Waardenburg (from Cairns) in ensuring veteran star Chris Goulding has a chance for another ring. Despite early injury issues, the signs are promising, with United claiming the NBL Blitz pre-season tournament title. Goulding, entering his 12th season with the franchise, said Chance had impressed through building relationships and his game craft.



“I don’t want to say surprised me, but what’s been really great has been his attention to detail, his intent to get clarity, and how steadfast he is in what he believes in, and what he wants us to do and how he thinks we can be successful in that. He’s steadfast in that,” Goulding said. San Antonio Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama. Getty Images Ingles, the NBA and Boomers veteran, is ready after a pre-season calf issue, and has delivered with his intangibles off the court in showing the younger players what is required to succeed at the top level. Anthony, a former teammate of Ingles with the Orlando Magic, will provide speed and shooting. Perth-product Travers, a former Cleveland Cavalier, will again play multiple roles in his return to the club. Oduro was with the New Orleans Pelicans last season, while Waardenburg is an athletic forward who can shoot from outside. Loading

World.title: Only one of the Serong boys will reach the grand final this year. Their mum is already taking sides
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Only one of the Serong boys will reach the grand final this year. Their mum is already taking sides Andrew Wu September 18, 2026 — 7:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

On Friday night at the SCG, Tania and Jamie Serong and their family will gather in the Fremantle rooms for a presentation in recognition of their son Caleb’s 150th game for the Dockers. They’ll then head in separate directions. While Tania takes her seat in the stands among the Fremantle friends and families’ section, her husband will make his way onto the hallowed turf of the SCG to be part of a guard of honour for Sydney’s players as they run onto the field. Jai and Caleb Serong (right) as kids. If you think Matthew Pavlich, the Fremantle great turned Sydney chief executive, was conflicted, spare a thought for the Serongs, whose sons Caleb and Jai go head-to-head for a grand final berth.



Unlike just about everyone else in the sold-out crowd on Friday night, the Serongs can’t lose, no matter what the result is. But they can’t win either. “I’m really torn,” Jamie told this masthead this week. “No matter how you look at it, you’ll have one extremely happy young boy, and one devastated young boy. It’s going to be a challenge on that front.” Caleb Serong is one of the AFL’s premier midfielders. Getty Images Sibling rivalry in September is not uncommon in the AFL. The Hill brothers, Brad and Stephen for Hawthorn and Fremantle respectively – squared off in the 2013 grand final. Brothers Reid (Sam and Ben) and Shaw (Rhyce and Shaw) met in the preliminary final the year earlier, as did the Selwoods (Joel for Geelong, and Scott and the late Adam for West Coast) in 2011. This will be the third time Caleb and Jai will play against each other at AFL level, but never have the stakes been so high.



The match will be a family reunion of sorts. Almost 20 of them will be there, including the boys’ grandfather and aunt from Mum’s side, Caleb’s wife Chloe and her parents, and Jai’s girlfriend and her sister. View post on X The brothers have dismissed the occasion as just another game, and they’ll treat each other as just another opponent, but it’s not as straightforward for their parents. This has not been an easy week for them. For Tania, there has been an underlying nervousness since it became apparent a fortnight ago the two clubs could meet in a preliminary final. “It’s a wonderful problem to have, but it’s still intense,” Tania said.



Jai Serong has fast become a key component for the Swans, given his versatility in playing a number of roles. Sam Mooy When their boys play, the Serongs have a foot in each camp. Mum will sit with one club, Dad the other. When Fremantle hosted Sydney in July, Jamie watched the game with the Dockers families as he had not seen them for a while, and Tania was with the Swans. They decided then they would swap for the next match-up. While most mothers sit on the fence, Tania’s allegiances are firmly with the Dockers. No, she does not have a favourite son, but as neutrality is difficult for her, she has decided she would be all-in behind the team she is sitting with. The next day, she’ll swap colours and watch the replay from the point of view of the other team, to appreciate the other perspective.



“I’ve tried to watch games as a neutral – you don’t watch anything, you’re off in fairy land, [and] you can’t ground into the game,” Tania said. “It’s really important to watch the game on one side or the other. “You can’t actually barrack for two teams at once. This week, I’m purple.” The exception will be if Jai is lining up for the winning goal after the siren. “I would be with the one kicking – that’s a special moment,” Tania said. “If you have the opportunity, take it.” Tania, though, won’t be wearing the Fremantle colours, nor will the couple be putting on split scarves. That drew too many weird looks, she said. Instead, she will wear a badge for both sons, one on each side, as her show of support.



Jame and Tania Serong will have their allegiances split on Friday night. Usually, when only one son is playing, Tania takes her eye off the ball to keep watch on him. When the two clubs last met – and she was sitting with the Swans – she did not know where Caleb was until he had the ball. “A couple of times I checked what his stats were like to keep an eye on how he was going,” Tania said. ‘You can’t actually barrack for two teams at once. This week, I’m purple.’ Caleb and Jai Serong’s mum, Tania Jamie has a different approach. Earlier this year, he found himself applauding Fremantle more, only because they scored more in a come-from-behind victory.



“I do have a real weird feeling, it’s not how much I support but how much I don’t get angry,” Jamie said. “I can get frustrated if the opposition’s winning. Last week, I was holding my breath for a quarter and a half. I don’t get as stressed because the opposition I have a lot of love for.” Jai has played primarily on the wing but, after the late-season upheaval in the Swans team, spent much of the qualifying final in the centre square, which is Caleb’s natural habitat. Even if Jai is not given the job of shadowing his brother, they will undoubtedly draw swords at some point. As kids, the pair, separated by two years and seven days, were fierce competitors. Throw in youngest brother Liam, a talented footballer himself in the VFL and at local level, and there was little peace for mum and dad.



“Cricket was the worst,” Tania said. “You’d think, ‘Oh good, they’re playing cricket’, then within an over, someone had cracked it, someone wasn’t out. It was all very competitive. “There were lots of fights. They’d get physical. You’d have to react quickly. Otherwise it would escalate pretty quickly. I just herded them to different places. It was full on, it was very busy.” View post on X For much of their childhoods, Caleb had the size advantage until he reached 15, when Jai had a growth spurt. Caleb is now listed at 180 centimetres, 13cm shorter than Jai. For competitive siblings, having a taller younger brother adds complexities at that age. “As you can imagine, everyone else had a comment on it,” Tania said. “‘Oh your brother is getting taller than you’.”



Jai, both parents say, would not often stir up his brother, but when he did, he would make it count. Related Article AFL 2026 AFL preliminary final teams and expert tips: Skipper’s replacement named; Lions make a key call “Jai would say stuff like, ‘What’s it like down there?’,” Jamie said. In the main, Caleb had come to terms with his lot though he would occasionally wonder why he had missed out on that part of the genetic lottery. “I honestly think Caleb was hoping there was more growth coming,” Jamie said. “I must admit there would be the odd time when Jai passed him, there’d be only me and Tania around, and he’d look at us and go, ‘What the hell happened? Where’s my height?’



“Caleb didn’t mind. I suppose he’d talk it off and come up with some other way he was better than Jai.” As footballers, their careers have taken different paths. Caleb was a top-10 draft pick who played just about immediately, has multiple All-Australian and best-and-fairest awards. Jai, a late selection, has fought tooth and nail for his 33 games, moving to a second club for greater opportunities. They have played plenty of cricket together, but the only times they have been on the same footy field have been as opponents. They could easily have been teammates. Hawthorn selected Jai with pick 53 in 2021. Fremantle had pick 54. Jamie got a call after the draft from Dockers coach Justin Longmuir, chief executive Simon Garlick and then footy boss Peter Bell apologising, telling him they would have taken him with the next selection. “Jai would say stuff like, ‘What’s it like down there?’” Jamie Serong on a rare sledge from Jai to his older, “little” brother Caleb



The Dockers were rebuffed again last year when Jai, coming off back-to-back best and fairests with Hawthorn’s VFL team Box Hill, chose to head north rather than west. Mum, Dad and older brother would have loved to see Jai don the purple with Caleb, but understood the decision. Editor's pick AFL 2026 Depleted, doubted and written off, yet somehow the Swans are just one win from another grand final “We were proud,” Jamie said. “He didn’t get selfish but thought about where he fit the best and what gave him the best opportunity to succeed. “You did think to yourself if they were both in the one place, you know the brothers would like to play together. Once again, Caleb was great with that. He knew why Jai did it and was totally happy for him.” For the parents, it would have eased the logistical challenges that come with supporting three sons who play football in three states, sometimes at the same time.



They do not get to many games together, outside of the rare occasions the Dockers play in Melbourne. In a normal year, Tania would travel to Perth about five times, preferably during a point in the season when the Dockers play at home on consecutive weeks so she can spend more time with her son. But this has not been a normal year for the family. In February, Jamie was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma. He’s happy to for his health battle to be made public as long as it does not overshadow his boys’ achievements. He has finished chemotherapy with radiation therapy to come. The illness has made it challenging to fly interstate too often for games, Jamie said. Travel will not be an issue for them in grand final week, barring injury or suspension to the winning brother.

World.title: ASX set to rise, Wall Street climbs as oil prices slide, bond market pressure eases; UK keeps rates on hold
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise, Wall Street climbs as oil prices slide, bond market pressure eases; UK keeps rates on hold Stan Choe Updated September 18, 2026 — 6:25am ,first published 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The US stock market rallied to its best day in six weeks after falling oil prices and easing pressure from the bond market helped Wall Street reverse many of its moves from the prior day. The S&P 500 jumped 1.1 per cent for just its second rise in the last nine days. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 316 points, or 0.6 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.7 per cent. Wall Street’s benchmark index is on track for just its second gain in the last nine sessions. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 4.57am AEST pointing to a gain of 57 points, or 0.7 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.4 per cent on Thursday. The Australian dollar was stronger at US71.11¢. US stocks got a boost after the price for a barrel of Brent crude oil slid 1 per cent to settle at $US104.82. That’s down from the nearly $US110 it reached earlier in the week on worries that the war with Iran will keep oil bottled up in the Middle East instead of going to customers worldwide.



Brent is of course still much more expensive than the $US72 per barrel that it cost earlier this summer, but Thursday’s drop helped pull yields lower in the bond market and removed some pressure on stocks. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93 per cent from 5.01 per cent late Wednesday. Related Article Aviation Qantas ground staff set to strike over ‘Joyce-era’ bargaining agreements Higher yields make it more expensive for everyone to borrow money, from the US government to people looking to buy houses to businesses wanting to build data centers. That in turn slows the economy. The Federal Reserve on Wednesday raised the short-term interest rate that it controls, the federal funds rate, by a quarter of a percentage point for its first hike in more than three years. Officials also signalled they may raise the federal funds rate one more time this year as they try to get the nation’s high inflation under control. The signals sent Wall Street on a roller coaster. Stocks initially remained higher for the day after the Fed made its announcement Wednesday. They then slid sharply before recovering a chunk of the losses before trading ended.



On the upside for markets, the shift to higher interest rates built confidence that the Fed is committed to getting inflation back to its target of 2 per cent. Questions had begun to bubble earlier about whether it would feel pressure from President Donald Trump, who is calling for lower interest rates. And the short-term cost of pain for the economy could be worth it if it gets inflation under control following years of its staying too high. On the downside for markets, higher rates undercut prices for stocks and other investments. When investors earn more in interest from bonds, which are considered safer investments, they’re less willing to pay high prices for other investments. That’s beyond the slowing effect that higher rates have on the economy in hopes of removing fuel for inflation. Some reports on Thursday signalled the US economy may be strong enough to withstand higher interest rates. One said fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week. Another said that manufacturing growth in the mid-Atlantic region was stronger than economists expected. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday that a strengthening economy is one of the reasons Fed officials moved to raise interest rates after keeping them on hold earlier this year. He also cited “geopolitics,” along with the threat that the increases in prices it’s causing could filter out and push up inflation elsewhere. That’s likely a nod to the war with Iran and its effect on oil prices.



On Wall Street, stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry continued to rebound following their worldwide slide on Monday. Nvidia climbed 2.5 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices rose 6.4 per cent. That was even though OpenAI disclosed six more reports of “unexpected or concerning” behavior in AI models. Leaders of the AI industry over the weekend called for a slowdown in development to address safety issues for humanity Stocks of several homebuilders also rose, even though a report showed the industry broke ground on fewer new homes last month than economists expected. The housing industry has been one of the hardest hit by the climb for the 10-year Treasury’s yield, which topped 5 per cent this week for the first time since 2023 and has pulled mortgage rates higher. Thursday’s ease in yields helped D.R. Horton rise 1.5 per cent, while PulteGroup added 1.1 per cent. Rival Lennar erased an early loss and climbed 1.7 per cent after reporting weaker profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. All told, the S&P 500 rose 85.95 points to 7,637.76. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 316.14 to 51,778.04, and the Nasdaq composite rallied 439.87 to 26,418.30.
